And the Qur'an brought this more than fourteen centuries ago.

The meaning of ﴿We would bring it forth﴾ (Al-Anbiya', 21:47) is: for them or against them. If it is in their favor, they will know that God does not wrong them, and He searches for them for the least of good. If it is against them, they will know that God takes account of everything thoroughly. The mustard seed, in its smallness, indicates volume, and the word (mithqal, "weight") indicates weight; thus both volume and weight are combined in it. Then the Exalted concludes this matter with: ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ (Al-Anbiya', 21:47). No one is as skilled at this matter or as precise in examining it as we are. We have no heedlessness, but precision and exact control of the standards of reckoning.

Do not think that the matter of reckoning and the balance is easy, such that you can reach complete precision however many precautions you take. You are human, and you cannot weigh with exact precision, because the iron standard by which you weigh is subject to increase or decrease in use. Dust may accumulate on it, and a drop of oil may fall on it, for example, and over time the standard increases even slightly, which benefits the one being weighed. Or the opposite may happen: the balance decreases through contact with things. You may look, for example, at a door handle and see it shining in contrast to what surrounds it. So any contact or friction with things diminishes them.

Even with modern balances that guarantee you the highest degrees of precision, human nature cannot give ultimate exactness. This is the meaning of ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ (Al-Ahzab, 33:39), and ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ (Al-Anbiya', 21:47), because His standard, the Exalted, does not vary, does not forget anything, and is not heedless of anything.

<sup>1</sup> The Imam Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari said in his book (Fath al-Rahman bi-kashf ma yaltabis fi al-Qur'an) (p. 405): (He linked the setting up of the balance with the raising of the heaven, because He enumerated His blessings upon His servants, and among the greatest of them is the balance, which is justice, by which the order and stability of the world exist.)

<sup>2</sup> From Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said: (Indeed My awliya' (close ones) on the Day of Resurrection are the pious, even if their lineage is more distant than another's lineage. The people will not come with deeds while you come with worldly things you carry upon your necks, and you say: "O Muhammad!" and I will say: "Thus," and I will turn away from him.) Narrated by Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunnah (1/94).

<sup>3</sup> From Hudhayfah, who said: I came to the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, while al-Abbas was sitting on his right and Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, on his left. He said: "O Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, work for God's good, for I cannot avail you anything from God on the Day of Resurrection." Cited by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id (1/49) and attributed to al-Bazzar.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion (al-Furqan), and a light and a reminder for the God-conscious.﴾ (21:48)

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wishes to console His Messenger ﷺ and lighten for him what he encountered from his people. So He mentions to him examples of his brothers, the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm)(1), who were persecuted by their peoples and harmed, so that the Messenger of Allah's mission would be made easier, and the harm of his people would not turn him away from his goal toward his Lord.

He began with Moses ﵇ because he is among the Messengers who exerted the most effort in their call, for Moses toiled with the believers in him, let alone the disbelievers in him. So He said, glory be to Him: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion...﴾ (21:48) (al-Anbiya'). Because their message was one, and they were partners in it: ﴿And my brother Aaron is more eloquent in speech than me...﴾ (28:34) (al-Qasas), and He said: ﴿Strengthen my back through him (31) and make him a partner in my affair (32)﴾ (Ta-Ha).

Al-Furqan: it is the strong distinguisher between two things. For the increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning, as you say: "Allah forgave so-and-so, forgiveness (ghufran)," and you say: "I read a reading (qira'a)," and "I recited the Qur'an (qur'an)." Reading is not one, and not every book is read.

Al-Furqan is also one of the names of the Qur'an: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ (25:1) (al-Furqan).

So al-Furqan, then, is a verbal noun that denotes intensification. You say: "faraqa, tafriqan and furqanan." The addition of the alif and nun indicates an increase in meaning, and that the separation in this matter is a grand and clear separation. For when you separate between two things whose matter is simple, you call this a farq (separation). But when you separate between two things, and there results from that a danger in the formation of society and a danger in the movement of life, this is a furqan. Therefore the Qur'an was named al-Furqan, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

From al-Furqan is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqanan)...﴾ (8:29) (al-Anfal). The fear of Allah is only achieved by carrying out His commands and teachings contained in the Qur'an that was revealed to Muhammad. And al-Furqan here means: a light by which you distinguish between things and differentiate between similar matters.

In proportion to how much you fear Allah by following the first Criterion, He will grant you the second Criterion, and there will form in you the insight of the believer (firasat al-mu'min) and his perception, and illuminations will descend upon you that aid the believer when he falls into a predicament.

Do you not see that they say: "So-and-so is intelligent, so-and-so has quick wit (hadir al-badiha)." That is: he brings to mind distant things and benefits from them in the present moment, and this is from Allah's granting success to him, and a result of his perception and insight. The Arabs used to give as an example of insight and intelligence Iyas ibn Mu'awiya, until the poet(2) said:

The boldness of 'Amr with the generosity of Hatim,
With the forbearance of al-Ahnaf and the intelligence of Iyas.

It is narrated that the Abbasid caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, when he wanted to perform the Hajj to the House of Allah for the last time, was informed that Sufyan al-Thawri(3) was belittling and criticizing him and accusing him of tyranny. He said: "I will make Hajj this year, and I want to see him crucified in Makkah." The news reached the people of Makkah. Sufyan al-Thawri was residing there with a group of his companions from the Sufis and the people of faith, among them Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, and the two of them would pamper al-Thawri and take pride in him.

One day the three were in the mosque, and al-Thawri was lying down between his two companions, placing his head in the lap of one of them and his feet in the lap of the other. The news of al-Mansur and his statement had reached them. Ibn 'Uyayna and al-Fudayl pleaded with Shaykh al-Thawri: "O Sufyan, do not disgrace us, and hide yourself so that he does not see you. For if al-Mansur gets hold of you and carries out his threat, the people's belief in those attributed to Allah will weaken."

Here al-Thawri said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, he will not enter it." And indeed al-Mansur entered Makkah from the direction of al-Hajun, and his mount stumbled with him while he was at the outskirts of Makkah, so he fell and was injured with a fracture, and died on the spot. Al-Mansur entered Makkah carried, and they brought him to the Sacred Mosque, where al-Thawri prayed over him.

This is the Criterion, the light, the insight, and the firasa of the believer who sees by the light of Allah, and does not act in any of his affairs except by His guidance.

It is also narrated that the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi entered the Ka'ba, and found a young boy about sixteen or seventeen years old, around whom four hundred elderly shaykhs of beards, dignity and gravity were gathered, while the boy was giving them a lesson. Al-Mahdi was amazed and said: "Fie upon these sa'anin (i.e., beards), is there not among them one who would come forward?!" Then he approached the boy wishing to rebuke and reprimand him, and said to him: "How old are you, boy?" The boy said: "My age is the age of Usama ibn Zayd when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed him commander of an army in which were Abu Bakr and Umar." So al-Mahdi, acknowledging his intelligence and his worthiness for this position, said: "May Allah bless you."

So al-Furqan, then, is used only for great and momentous matters, whether what was revealed to Moses or what was revealed to Muhammad. However, al-Furqan has become a proper name for the Qur'an. There is a difference between a proper name and a descriptive term: everything that distinguishes between truth and falsehood you may describe as a furqan, but when it is named as such, it refers to the Qur'an.

The one who reflects on the root (f-r-q) in the Qur'an finds that it has a role in the story of Moses ﵇. The first verse of his story: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you...﴾ (2:50) (al-Baqara).

Al-farq (separation) is to divide between a continuous thing while the thing is different. In the science of arithmetic they say: mixing and blending. There is a difference between separating things that are mixed, such as oranges, apples and grapes, and separating them when they are a blend of juice, interpenetrated until they have become one thing.

Thus: the splitting of the sea for Moses ﵇ was not merely a farq, but a furqan, because the greatest kinds of division is to split a flowing thing into two parts, each part like a mighty mountain(4). And who can accomplish this matter but Allah?

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and a light and a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ (21:48) (al-Anbiya'). That is: a light that guides people to the paths of their lives without ruin; otherwise how would they walk the roads of life? If a person walks without guidance, either he collides with someone stronger than him and is himself broken, or he collides with someone weaker and breaks him. So light is important and necessary in the journey of a human being, and by it he is guided to the safe movement of life, and strives upon clear evidence, so he neither tires himself nor tires others.

﴿And a reminder...﴾ (21:48) (al-Anbiya'). That is: it reminds the heedless. For if heedlessnesses accumulate, they become the rust (ran) that veils vision and blinds insight. Therefore when the Prophet ﷺ described the heedlessness of people he said: "Trials are presented to hearts like a mat, strand by strand."

In another narration: "ʿawdhan ʿawdhan" (strand by strand)(5), meaning: he seeks refuge with Allah that this should happen to a believer. Have you seen the mat-maker when he joins strand to strand until the mat is formed? Thus trials are presented to us. If reminder comes at the beginning, it removes the heedlessness in you, so heedlessnesses do not accumulate upon you.

(Whatever heart absorbs them – meaning accepts them – strand after strand, a black spot is marked upon it, and whatever heart rejects them, a white spot is marked upon it, until there are two hearts: one white like smooth stone, which no trial harms as long as the heavens and earth endure, and one black like an inverted cup – meaning upside down – which knows no good and denies no evil.)(6)

They said: this is the rust of which Allah says: ﴿Nay, but rust has covered their hearts from what they used to earn﴾ (83:14) (al-Mutaffifin). And remembrance is what polishes this rust.

﴿And a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ (21:48) (al-Anbiya'). And among their attributes is that they are:

﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾ (21:49).

1 He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So be patient as the Messengers of firm resolve were patient...﴾ (46:35) (al-Ahqaf). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (4/172): "They have differed about the enumeration of the ulu al-'azm into several opinions, the best known of which is that they are: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and the seal of the prophets, all of them Muhammad ﷺ. It may be that what is meant by ulu al-'azm is all the Messengers, so that 'min' in His saying 'from the Messengers' is explanatory of the category, and Allah knows best."
2 He is Abu Tammam Habib ibn Aws al-Ta'i, born in a village of the villages of Syria (180 AH), raised in humble circumstances, where he worked as a young apprentice to a weaver. He died in the year 231 AH at the age of 51.
3 He is Sufyan ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Thawri, of Mudar, Abu 'Abd Allah, Commander of the Believers in hadith, born in Kufa (97 AH). He was the master of the people of his time in the sciences of religion and piety. Al-Mansur the Abbasid courted him to take up rule, but he refused. He died in hiding in Basra from al-Mahdi in the year 161 AH (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 3/104).
4 Al-tawd: the high, firm mountain. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So He split, and each part was like a mighty mountain (63)﴾ (al-Shu'ara').
5 Ibn al-Athir said: it is narrated with a dhal with a dot, as if he sought refuge from trials. (Lisan al-Arab – root: '-w-dh).
6 Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih (144), Kitab al-Iman, and Ahmad in his Musnad (5/386, 405), from the hadith of Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman ﵁.

Al-Khashya: fear accompanied by reverence and awe. One may fear something while also disliking or despising it. Khashya is like fearing your father or your teacher, that he might see you falling short, and feeling shame before him when he sees you in a state of shortcoming. So the meaning of fearing Allah is that you fear being lacking in what He has asked of you and what He has charged you with, because His standards, exalted be He, are high, and some of them may have escaped you.

In another place the Truthful (al-Haqq), glorified be He, explains this matter, saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah...﴾ (35:28). Why? Because they are the most knowing of Allah and of His wisdom in His creation. Whenever the realities and secrets of the universe are unveiled to them, their fear of Allah increases, and it includes awe and veneration. Therefore He said of them: ﴿They fear their Lord above them...﴾ (16:50), meaning: above them and over their heads, yet with love and awe.

As for the meaning of ﴿unseen (bil-ghayb)...﴾ (21:49): they fear Allah even though they do not see Him with their eyes. They see Him only in the traces of His creation. Or bil-ghayb means the unseen matters that they do not witness, but after Allah informs them of them, they become, after Allah's informing, as though they were a scene before them that they see with their own eyes.

Or the meaning may be: they fear their Lord in their privacy away from people, so the awe of Allah and good manners toward Him accompany them even in their seclusion and solitude. This is unlike one who displays such conduct before people out of showing off, such as Nimrod in his privacy.

And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and they are apprehensive of the Hour...﴾ (21:49). Ishfaq also means fear, but it is a fear accompanied by caution regarding what one fears. Fear of Allah is accompanied by awe, and fear of the Hour is accompanied by caution about it, lest it come upon them before they have fully prepared themselves for it, a preparation that would gladden them with Allah's reward on the hour they meet Him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 50:

Meaning: just as the Torah came as a reminder (dhikran) [21:48], so too the Qur'an that was sent down to you, O Muhammad, is a reminder (dhikr), but it is a ﴿blessed reminder﴾ [21:50]. People say: "This is a blessed thing," meaning: it contains blessing (barakah). Blessing in a thing means that it gives more good than one expects from it.

Just as the Prophet (ﷺ) would give his Companions to drink from one large bowl (qa'b) of milk, and would feed the whole army from a small, meager amount of food. You hear people say: "So-and-so's salary is small, yet he and his children live in such-and-such a way," and we say: "Because God blesses this little."

So the meaning of ﴿a blessed reminder﴾ [21:50] is: it contains good beyond what you imagine. Beware of saying that it is merely a book of rulings and obligations. The Qur'an has the quality of eternity, and it contains secrets without end. Its blessing encompasses all aspects and all fields until the Hour arrives. However much we repeat its verses, we find them beautiful, evocative and expressive. Every age brings something new; it does not wear out through repeated recitation, and its wonders do not cease. It is blessed because the good in it extends beyond the age of the Messenger (ﷺ) and all ages, lifetimes and centuries, giving each day a new secret from the secrets of its Speaker, glory be to Him.

Therefore: the Qur'an is a ﴿blessed reminder﴾ [21:50], because the goods it contains extend beyond the age in which it was revealed, and beyond every lifetime and every century, giving each day a new hue of the secrets of its Speaker and the one who utters it. Hence, after this, He marvels at the people's denial of it: ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ [21:50]. Such a statement is denied.

We have already explained their views about the Qur'an.

Some of them said: it is sorcery; some said: it is poetry; some said: it is falsehoods and the fables of the ancients. All of this is bankruptcy of argument, a pursuit with no meaning, and evidence of the contradiction of their thoughts.

Did they not say themselves: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?﴾ [43:31]. So they know the Qur'an's truth and its standing, and that it is from God, and they do not object to it in anything; their objection is only to the one who brought the Qur'an. In this is evidence that they lack alertness in their heedlessness.

And reflect on: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ [21:50]. He did not say "this Qur'an," as if it is only pointed to as the Qur'an.

1 Qa'b: a large, thick bowl; it is said: a hollowed wooden bowl, which quenches a man's thirst. (Lisan al-'Arab, root q-‘-b.)
2 Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih (4152), and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-nubuwwah (4/115), from the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came on the day of the tree at al-Hudaybiyyah with water in a tur (vessel), placed his hand in it, and the water began to gush out from between his fingers like springs. He said: "We drank, and we had enough, and it sufficed us." It was said to Jabir: "How many were you?" He said: "Even if we had been a hundred thousand, it would have sufficed us; we were fifteen hundred."
3 From Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended [at the place] during the peace treaty with Quraysh, my companions said to the Prophet: "O Messenger of Allah, if we slaughter from our backs and eat from their meat and fat, and drink from the broth, we will be in the morning tomorrow when we go out to them, and we will have strength." He said: "No, but bring me what remains of your provisions." They spread out leather mats and poured upon them the remainder of what was left of their provisions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked blessing upon them, and they ate until they were full, then they wrapped up the leftovers of their provisions in their saddlebags. Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (Kitab al-Luqatah, Bab istihbab khalt al-azwad idha qallat). Also recorded by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-nubuwwah (4/120).

We observe that the Exalted One began His consolation of His Messenger ﷺ by mentioning a portion of the story of Musa (Moses), then followed it with the story of Ibrahim (Abraham), although Ibrahim (peace be upon him) preceded Musa. Why? They said: because Musa had a direct connection with the Jews and was close to them, and the Jews with him were people of dispute and obstinacy.

As for the meaning of ﴿rushdahu﴾ ("his right guidance", 21:51): al-rushd (rectitude, right guidance) is the mind's attainment of what is most perfect in goodness and highest in virtue, such that after goodness there does not come corruption, nor after good does evil follow, and it does not deliver you from height to descent. This is rushd. But if apparent goodness draws you into corruption, or good delivers you to evil, there is no rushd in that.

Now listen to them speaking of the fine arts, and seeking people's favour with glittering slogans that have pleased the people, to the point that their boldness has reached the extent that they say of dancing: it is a refined and beautiful art. Glory be to God! Dancing, as you say, if it were truly refined and beautiful and remained so to the end of the road, and did not sink into something ugly and base — what happens when a man sits before a dancer who displays of her charms and movements what his wife does not do well at home? How many homes have been ruined and families destroyed because of a dancer! So what refinement is this? And what beauty is there in this art?!

Therefore Imam ʿAli — may God honour his face — summed up this matter, saying: "There is no evil after which there is Paradise, and no good after which there is Hellfire."

So: a person must be mindful of rushd, which is the mind's attainment of the highest good, or the highest perfection, or the highest goodness. This rushd has two directions: rushd of the body (rushd al-bunya), and rushd of meaning (rushd al-maʿna).

Rushd of the body: it is the completion of a person's formation such that every organ performs its function. This does not occur except after the age of puberty (sin al-bulugh), and the Creator, glory be to Him, made the maturity of the reproductive organs a sign of the completion of this rushd, when a person becomes able to beget his like.

This is evident in fruits, whose taste is not sweet except after they ripen and their seed is complete so as to be fit for germination if you plant it. This is from the wisdom of the Creator — glory be to Him and exalted is He — that we eat the fruit and preserve its species through its good seed. But if the fruit were ready for eating before its seed ripened, we would eat the existing fruits and not preserve its species, and it would become extinct.

Likewise, from God's wisdom is that when the fruit is ripe and has not found someone to pick it, it falls of its own accord and renews its cycle in life.

And for a matter, God made legal responsibility (taklif) to follow puberty. For if He had imposed it upon you before puberty, you would find in the obligations a prohibition of some matters that you do not know or comprehend. You might object to your Lord: "How shall I act, O Lord, when this instinct has come upon me and done to me such and such?"

Every instrument and organ in the human body has a rushd suited to it, and a growth suited to its formation. For example, the child's eye, mouth and fingers all grow in a manner appropriate to the child's formation.

As for the teeth, there is profound wisdom from the Creator, Mighty and Majestic. For the child, in the stage in which he cannot clean his teeth himself, and neither can another easily clean them, He made for him a spare set of teeth that accompanies him in his youth, called the milk teeth (al-asnan al-labaniyya). Then, when he grows up and becomes able to clean his teeth himself, God replaces them with another set that accompanies him throughout his life.

There is also a higher rushd: a rushd of intellect and mind, in which reason and thinking mature and the mind that chooses and weighs among alternatives is complete. A person may attain the rushd of his physical body without his intellect and thinking being complete. In this case we do not enable him to dispose of his affairs until we test him, to know the extent of his good management of what he owns. If he succeeds in the test, we give him his wealth, to dispose of it as the words of the Exalted One state:

﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them rushd, deliver to them their property...﴾ (4:6). That is: do not wait until he grows up and then give him his wealth to do with as he wishes without experience or practice. Rather, you test him and involve him in the midst of life and its struggle, so that he grows up skilled and capable of sound disposal.

In another verse the Exalted said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property...﴾ (4:5), because if they reach physical rushd but not mental rushd, and beware of saying: "It is his property; he disposes of it as he wishes." For the foolish has no property, as evidenced by ﴿do not give the foolish your property﴾; He did not say "their property." You are the custodian of it, guarding it as though it were yours, and you are accountable for it before God, and the property of the foolish is not his unless he disposes of it well.

And of rushd is what the Qur'an calls al-ashudd: ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu) and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, enable me (awzi'ni) to be thankful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents...﴾ (46:15).

Al-ashudd is the attainment of the peak of rushd. He said here "forty years," although we have mentioned that a person reaches rushd of the body and rushd of the mind after puberty, around the fifteenth year. So whoever has not attained rushd by forty, there is no hope for him, and the Fire is more fitting for him. For when he disbelieves or deviates from the path in the prime of his youth and strength, we say: the wildness of youth, desire, adolescence, and the rest of these excuses. But when he reaches forty, what is his excuse?

And if he has not received the principles of rushd in his childhood and youth, there is no doubt that during forty years he will find in life's events a reality that guides him against his will, for he sees his deeds and their consequences, his errors and his falls, and he should take from them a practical and theoretical lesson in rushd.

Of this are the contemporary terms we hear, such as they say: "political rushd" and they say: "rationalization of consumption" (tarshid al-istihlak). What is the meaning of these terms? Their meaning is that the events of life and its experiences, and the lack of rushd in their course, have bitten people, and driven them to think of rationalization that would remove this corruption.

So: rushd is for the self, and tarshid is for others, as we do in rationalizing the consumption of wheat, for example, which we used to feed to livestock, until we no longer found it. Therefore we began rationalizing the consumption of bread loaves and came to divide one into four parts, and eat with calculation, and waste nothing; what remains stays clean and we eat it at another meal.

The baker himself may not have rationalization, so he takes the loaf out before it is fully baked, and you find it dough, all of it soft inside; then the wise housewife comes and opens the loaf before placing it on the table, takes out this soft part, gathers it, toasts it in the oven, and makes another food from it.

What is said of "rationalizing bread" is said of "rationalizing water," and the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded us to rationalize the consumption of water, even in ablution, which is an act of nearness to God.

This rushd we have described is the rushd of every sensible person other than the Messengers: that he is guided to the matters of his life and disposes of them soundly. Rather, the result of this righteousness is in this world; but the Messengers have another rushd, a higher rushd for this world and the Hereafter, and this is a gift from God to the Messengers.

The Exalted said concerning Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿And We had already given Ibrahim his rushd before, and We were knowing of him﴾ (21:51). It is as though Ibrahim's rushd was not subject to these rules, nor tied to puberty or prophethood, but was a rushd preceding its time since he was a child, contemplating the stars and seeking his Lord:

﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said: This is my lord. But when it set, he said: Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray. (77) Then when he saw the sun rising, he said: This is my lord; this is greater. But when it set, he said: O my people, I am free of what you associate (with God). (78)﴾ (6:77-78).

He – peace be upon him – was thus qualified for prophethood from his childhood, and when he was sent and received prophecy, the gifts of his rushd appeared when he was thrown into the fire, and Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him offering assistance, but Ibrahim said: "As for you, no." This was the first glad tidings of intellectual and doctrinal rushd in Ibrahim.

And concerning him the Exalted said: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them...﴾ (2:124). That is: He tested him in matters and he fulfilled them in the most perfect manner. Among them: He commanded him to raise the foundations of the House. It would have sufficed for Ibrahim to raise the foundations of the House as high as his hand could reach, but Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was keen that the matter be completed in the most perfect way, so he thought and devised to bring a stone and stand on it to raise the building by the height of the stone. His young son Isma'il would help him, handing him the stones, but the young boy's feet would slip as he lifted the stones to his father, so he devised a solution: he dug into the stone to the measure of his feet so that they would be fixed, and these two feet we still see today in the stone of Isma'il.

So: he had a passion for legal duties and eagerness to complete them.

And the Exalted's words: ﴿and We were knowing of him﴾ (21:51) are evident in His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ (6:124).

Footnote 1: Anasa al-shay': he perceived it and sensed it with his sight, or with his knowledge and thought. And His words: ﴿if you perceive in them rushd﴾ (4:6) mean: you know and perceive it with inner perception. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/37).

Footnote 2: awza'ahu an yafʿala kadha: he urged him and prompted him and incited him; or inspired him and guided him. The Exalted said: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be thankful...﴾ (46:15). That is: inspire me to thank You, drive me to it and make it beloved to me. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/334).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 52:

I.e.: Mention, O Muhammad, when Abraham said to his father and his people, ﴿What are these images (tamathil) that you are devoted to?﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:52).

Tamathil is the plural of timthal, which is derived from mithl or mathal. The mithl of a thing means its likeness and counterpart. They used to deliberately take objects that have bulk and shape them in the form of created things of God, such as the form of a human or an animal, out of stone, iron, wood or other materials, and they called it a timthal, and they set it up to be worshipped.

They would go to great lengths in this: this one of stone, that one of marble, this one small and that one large. They would sometimes place two gems in its eyes so that it would appear to the viewer that it has sight. These were varieties of artistry in this craft.

So Abraham, peace be upon him, says, reproachfully to his father and his people: ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:52).

The interrogative here is not in its literal sense; rather it is a rejecting interrogation that carries a tone of mockery, scorn and rebuke, and he must have put this question to them in a performative manner that suggests reproach.

We have previously discussed the meaning of (abihi) here and said: the intended meaning is his uncle, by the evidence of God's saying in another place: ﴿to his father Azar…﴾ (al-An'am 6:74). He began the matter with his father or uncle, who is the closest person to him, wishing to reassure people regarding what he calls them to, and that it is good; otherwise he would not have begun with his father.

Also, because the people may not have an effect of awe or love on him, whereas awe and love exist with respect to his father or uncle. Nevertheless, this awe did not prevent him from belittling their words and their false deeds, as came in the saying of God Most High:

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear may decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than God and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until God brings His command. And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:24).

The exegetes have paused at the preposition lam in God's saying ﴿lahā ʿākifūn﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:52), although the meaning is "they cling to worshipping them," as came in another verse: ﴿They came upon a people who cling to idols they had.﴾ (al-A'raf 7:138). Here it came with lam, so some said: the lam here means ʿalā (upon), so why did it shift from ʿalā to lam?

If we pay attention to the implications of the wording ﴿lahā ʿākifūn﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:52): we say, iʿtikāf is staying (al-iqamah). When someone is ʿākif in the mosque, it means he is staying in the mosque. So the word ʿākifūn alone conveys the meaning of ʿalā, i.e., for the benefit of these gods. As for lam, it is for something else: the lam here is the lam of ownership and benefit. They mentioned another example of it in God's saying: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings…﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:104).

Al-sijill (scroll) is the parchment and paper on which we write, and from it comes the saying "we sajjala such-and-such," meaning we write it in the scroll or paper so that it is preserved. The meaning of ﴿lil-kutub﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:104) is "the thing written," so it is as if the meaning is: We fold the paper over what has been written upon it.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾

So: they have no proof for their worship of these images, which they fashioned and set up with their own hands, except that they saw their fathers worshipping them. Their argument is blind imitation (taqlid), and had they had any argument grounded in the act itself, they would have stated it.

Elsewhere they said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and we are, upon their footsteps, guided.﴾ (al-Zukhruf) So: we criticise them for this imitation, and we criticise our fathers too. How, then, would Ibrahim's reply be?

The word ﴿ʿābidīn﴾ (al-Anbiya) here expresses that their worship of them is worship without understanding, because worship (ʿibadah) is the obedience of a worshipper to the commands of the one he worships. So what did the idols command them?

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says of Ibrahim that he said to his people:

﴿He said: "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error."﴾ (21:54)

He wanted to guide this foolishness, so he said: "You are in error, because you have imitated [others] in belief, and belief cannot be by imitation (taqlid); and your fathers, because they invented these matters and established them as a tradition for you."

It is strange that they would imitate their fathers in this particular matter and not in others. Otherwise, who would remain upon what his father was upon? We see every generation bringing forth something new that was not known to the previous generation.

For this reason they say: "People resemble their times more than they resemble their fathers." Every era has its own circumstances and its own advancements. You control your child while he is young: he eats, drinks and dresses according to what you wish. But when he grows up and matures, he has his own personality and independent thought. He chooses his own food and clothing, and the faculty (kulliyah) he enters, and perhaps he criticizes you in some matters.

So these people imitated their fathers in this matter and not in others. Why, then, in the matter of belief in particular do you hold fast to imitation? Had every generation come as an exact copy of its predecessor, the face of life would not have changed. This indicates that every generation has its own independent character and its own particular thought.

These people imitated their fathers in this worship and not in other matters, because a worship and religiosity without obligation, and gods without a method, do not constrict them in anything and do not forbid them anything of the desires to which they are accustomed. So it is a religiosity without accountability.

Therefore, the Truth, glory be to Him, answers them in two different styles. Once He says, exalted is He:
﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ (2:170)

And in another place He says, exalted is He:
﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ (5:104)

We note that the endings of the two verses differ: once, ﴿they do not reason anything…﴾ (2:170), and once ﴿they do not know anything…﴾ (5:104). Why?

They said: because the ending of each verse is suited to its beginning, and the beginnings of the two verses differ. In the first, they said ﴿Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon…﴾ (2:170), meaning one may follow this or that, without confining themselves to one thing.

In the second, they said ﴿Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon…﴾ (5:104), meaning: it is enough for us, and we want no addition to it, so they confined themselves to what they found their fathers upon.

Therefore, in the ending of the first He said ﴿they do not reason anything…﴾ (2:170), and in the ending of the second ﴿they do not know anything…﴾ (5:104), because the one who reasons is the one who is guided to a matter by himself.

As for the one who knows, he knows what he has reasoned out himself and what others have reasoned out. So the circle of knowledge ('ilm) is wider than the circle of reason ('aql), because reason is guided to a thing by itself, whereas knowledge takes the guidance of others.

Their response was: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us with the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ (21:55)

I mean: "Is this speech of yours serious, O Ibrahim, or are you joking with us?" It is as if they found it hard to believe that Ibrahim's words were in earnest, because they were far beyond their understanding.

Ibrahim responds: I have brought you the truth, which says that these idols are not to be worshipped, but that the one who deserves worship is Allah, the Lord of the heavens and the earth:

﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them...﴾ (Al-Anbiya', 21:56)

Here "bal" (rather, on the contrary) cancels what came before it and establishes the ruling for what follows. ﴿Who created them...﴾ (21:56) means: who created the heavens, the earth, the idols, and everything that exists.

﴿And I am among those who bear witness to that.﴾ (21:56) The witness (shahid) is the one who has been guided to the truth, as if he had seen it with his own eyes, and there is no "where" with the eye. He was also guided to the proof of this truth, so he said: I am a witness that your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and with me is the proof of this reality.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 57:

After what had passed between them of stubbornness and argument based on falsehood, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) swore an oath: ﴿By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols...﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:57). The "ta" here is for the oath (qasam).

﴿...I will surely plot against your idols...﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:57). Can idols be plotted against? Or is the meaning: "I will surely plot against you concerning your idols"? The idols, as a creation among the creatures of Allah, glorify Allah, and they thank Ibrahim for this deed.

How beautifully the poet has said on this meaning, speaking in the tongue of the stones in the Cave of Hira and the Cave of Thawr, where the stones were jealous of and envied Hira, because the Chosen Prophet (ﷺ) used to worship in it before the Prophethood. Hira was a witness to the worship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), taking pride in this companionship. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed in the Cave of Thawr during the Hijrah, Thawr rejoiced, because it had come to the same rank as Hira:

How often we envied Hira when you see the Spirit, the trustworthy one, visiting you with the lights.
Hira and Thawr have become equal, through both of them the kingdom of stones intercedes.
They worshipped us, and we are more worthy of worship than those who stand in the night prayers.
They took our silence as a proof against us, so we became fuel for their fire.

Because Allah said: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones...﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:24).

They have been unjust out of ignorance, just as they were unjust toward the son of Maryam and the disciples.
For the one who exceeds limits, his reward is his, and the one who exaggerates about him, the mercy of the Forgiving will save him.

Therefore, breaking the idols is not a plot against the idols, but against their worshippers who believe that they harm and benefit. It is as if Ibrahim (peace be upon him) establishes for these people the proof of the invalidity of idol worship, the practical proof that cannot be refuted. It is as though Ibrahim is saying in the tongue of his state: "When I break the idols, if I am upon falsehood, let them stop me and let them turn the axe away from my hand; and if I am upon truth, they will leave me to do what I do."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿...after you have turned away, retreating.﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:57). That is: after you have gone away from them, meaning: while they were heedless.

(Footnote 1: From the poetry of the Shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, in a qasida about the Hijrah.)

Then the Almighty says: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except for their biggest one, so that they might turn back to it.﴾

We notice here that the Qur'anic discourse omits what is understood from the speech, as in the story of Solomon, peace be upon him, and the hoopoe: ﴿Go with this letter of mine and drop it to them; then turn away from them and see what they return.﴾ (An-Naml) And the omission of what the hoopoe did, his journey to Bilqis, his dropping the letter to her, and that she took it and presented it to her counselors: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me."﴾ (An-Naml)

And the meaning of ﴿fragments﴾ (Q. 21:58) (al-Anbiya'): that is, scattered pieces and debris, after they had been assembled figures.

﴿Except for their biggest one﴾ (Q. 21:58) (al-Anbiya'): that is, he left it and did not smash it. They used to place the idols in a particular arrangement and "decor", such that the biggest one was in the middle with the small idols around it, meaning that it seemed to have authority over them and a standing among them. They would also place emerald (zabarjad) in its eye, so that whoever saw it imagined that it was looking at him.

And His saying: ﴿so that they might turn back to it﴾ (Q. 21:58) (al-Anbiya'): that they would ask it about what had happened to its young gods, the small ones, and why it did not defend them, especially since they found the axe on its shoulder.

Meaning: when they went to the place of worship where they worshipped their idols, they found them smashed, and they said: ﴿Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:59), because he transgressed against the gods and broke them, though they were sound.

So these gods cannot ward off harm from themselves. They should have paid attention to this matter: how can they accept worshipping them? If the wind had struck one of them, it would have broken him. The god would need someone to repair his arm, mend him and set him back in his place. So what kind of divinity is this whose rights they are defending?!

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 21, verse 60:

Meaning: some of them volunteered and said, "This is what we heard." It was for a people on a set day when they would go out to their temple and the place of their idols, and take their food and drink. It seems that it was a festival day for them. Azar had prepared for this day, and he wanted to take Ibrahim with him, so that the gods might attract him, and he would be guided and turn away from what he was in.

But Ibrahim, peace be upon him, claimed that he was sick and could not go out with them, so he said, ﴿Indeed, I am ill⁽¹⁾﴾ (al-Saffat 37:89). At that point Ibrahim resolved to smash their idols, and said: ﴿By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away, retreating﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:57). Some of the people heard him and informed them of what he had said.

﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them..."﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:60): the word "mention" here means in a bad sense as far as they were concerned. ﴿who is called Ibrahim﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:60): meaning, his name is Ibrahim, or when we call him we say, "O Ibrahim."

¹ Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ (al-Saffat 37:88–89). Qatadah said: "The Arabs say of one who reflects, 'He looked at the stars.'" Qatadah meant that he looked up at the sky, reflecting on what would distract them with it, and then said, ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾ (al-Saffat 37:89), i.e., weak. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 4/13).

Then the Truthful, Glorified be He, says: ﴿They said, "Then bring him before the eyes of the people, that they may bear witness."﴾

And the meaning of ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾ (Al-Anbiya): that is, in plain sight of them, so that they may witness him with their own eyes. ﴿that they may bear witness﴾ (Al-Anbiya): that is, that they may witness what we inflict upon him of punishment, so that no one else dares to do such a deed, and it becomes a lesson for others.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 62:

﴿They said: "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ (62):

Here too there is an omitted statement: they brought him, and then they asked him this question. The interrogative in ﴿Is it you who did this..﴾ (62) (al-Anbiya') is a question about the doer, because the act itself is clear and does not need to be questioned. Therefore they did not say "Did you do this, O Ibrahim?" but rather focused on the doer: ﴿Is it you who did this..﴾ (62) (al-Anbiya'). It is like when you say: "Did you build the house that you intended to build?" This is a question about the act, whereas "Is it you who built the house?" is about the doer, so the intended meaning is the doer.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 63:

It is as if he wants to extract from them an acknowledgment that this large idol does nothing, and then confronts them: "Why then do you worship them?"

Ibrahim's saying: ﴿Rather, it was their chief who did it, this one⁠—﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:63) contains rebuke and reproach for them, for he attributed the act to one who is incapable of it and could not have done it. Al-Zamakhshari (may Allah have mercy on him) gave an example of this: a man with beautiful handwriting and another who cannot write well. The latter sees a beautiful calligraphic panel and says to the first, "Are you the one who wrote this panel?" He replies, "No, rather you are the one who wrote it!!" as a rebuke and reproach to him.

Then Ibrahim openly tells them what he intends: ﴿So ask them, if they are able to speak.﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:63) They will not ask them, because they know their true state.

Al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 21, verse 64:

"They came to themselves" (tanabbahu wa 'adu ila 'uqulihim), i.e., they awakened and returned to their reason, and they spoke the truth: ﴿Indeed, you yourselves are the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:64). That is: by your worshipping these idols, while you know that they neither benefit nor harm, and neither see nor speak.

Thus they confronted themselves with this reality and exposed the falsehood of this worship. But this awakening will be at their own expense, and their loss through it will be great. This awakening will deprive them of the temporal authority under whose shadow they live, and from which they profit through what is offered to the idols. Therefore they quickly retreat and turn back on their heels, after reality has overcome them and they have remembered what this awakening would bring upon them.

Then, after they were confronted with the truth, ﴿they were turned upside down onto their heads﴾ (al-Anbiya', 65). The *naksah* (reversal) means that the high is brought to the low, and you certainly know this! They went back and said to him the same argument he had made against them: ﴿You know well that these cannot speak﴾ (al-Anbiya', 65). This is precisely *al-taghfil* (feigning heedlessness or making someone appear foolish).

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿He said: "Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?" (21:66)﴾:

Meaning: It cannot benefit you with anything if you worship it, and it cannot harm you with anything if you abandon its worship.

Uff: an interjection (ism fi'l, "noun standing for a verb") meaning "I am vexed." It is not a noun, nor a verb, nor a particle; rather, "uff" is a noun that signifies a verb, so it has in it something of the nominal and something of the verbal. For this reason they call it (al-Khalifa), because Arabic speech revolves around a noun, a verb, or a particle. Similar is hayhat: an interjection (ism fi'l) meaning "far off" or "too late." So Abraham (peace be upon him) expresses by this word, uff, his distress and vexation at what his people do of worshipping idols besides Allah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 68:

We note their saying: ﴿Burn him...﴾ (68) (al-Anbiya'): with the doubled letter, which indicates intensification. They did not say, for example, "uhriquhu" (burn him). They gathered together for this act, built a structure, placed fire in it, and remained for forty days kindling it (1) with everything that could catch fire. Thereby the heat of the fire became intense, so much so that a bird passing over this fire would fall roasted from its intense heat (2).

The evidence for this is that when they wanted to throw Ibrahim into the fire, they could not approach it because of the intensity of its scorching blaze, so they made a catapult (manjaniq) to hurl him into the fire from a distance.

And their saying: ﴿And support your gods...﴾ (68) (al-Anbiya'): according to their belief, it is as if the battle were between Ibrahim and the gods. In reality, the gods they worship are with Ibrahim and not against him. So the battle, then, is between Ibrahim and the worshippers of idols.

And their saying: ﴿If you are going to act...﴾ (68) (al-Anbiya'): meaning: if you are going to do anything to Ibrahim, then burn him.

1 Sajara al-tannur yasjuruhu sajran: he kindled and heated it. It was said: he filled it fully with fuel. (Lisan al-Arab, root: s-j-r)
2 Ibn Ishaq said: they gathered firewood for a month, then lit it, and it blazed and intensified, until a bird would pass by its sides and be burned by the intensity of its heat. (Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 6/4481)

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says concerning His rescuing Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from this burning: ﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim.﴾ (21:69).

This command came from the Most High, glorified is He, so that by means of a miracle He would break the prevailing laws of the cosmos. Only the Creator of a law can break it, as we said in the story of Musa, peace be upon him: water's law is fluidity and flowing through channels, and none can strip it of this property except its Creator. Therefore He split the sea for Musa, a splitting (furqan), as we said, each part like a mighty mountain. Thus none suspends the nature of things except the One who created them, for things were not created to have the power to sustain themselves; rather they are created to perform a task, and the One who created them for that task is able to strip them of their properties.

There is a difference between the act of the servant and the act of the Truth, glorified is He. Suppose you have a pistol in your hand, you are skilled at aiming, the target is before you, and you fire a bullet at the target. Do you have any control over it after that? Can you command it to swerve to the right or to the left?

But the Truth, glorified is He, controls it and directs it as He wills. For the Truth, glorified is He, created fire and created in it the property of burning, and He alone is able to strip this property from it, so that it becomes fire without burning. Fire has no self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) in itself.

For this reason some say: as soon as the command was issued, ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety...﴾ (21:69), every fire in the world was extinguished; then when He said ﴿upon Ibrahim﴾ (21:69), the matter became specific to Ibrahim's fire, to the exclusion of others, so the fires of the world were kindled again apart from this one. We note that the Truth, glorified is He, qualified coolness with safety, because absolute coolness would harm.

(1) Ibn 'Abbas said: Had He not followed "coolness" with "safety," Ibrahim would have died from its cold. Thus on that day no fire remained on earth except that it was extinguished, thinking that it was the one intended. Related by al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim (cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 5/640).

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾ (21:70)

The intended meaning of "scheme" (kayd) here is the matter of burning him. The meaning of kayd is a hidden plan against an enemy, so that he is unaware of what is being plotted against him and thus takes precautions against the matter. Kayd may be for the benefit of a thing, and it may be its opposite. In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus did We devise for Joseph...﴾ (12:76) it means for his benefit. He did not say "We schemed against Joseph" but "We schemed for him."

They have said about kayd that it is a sign of weakness and of inability to confront directly. The one who plots against another and conspires against him in secret does so only because he is unable to face him.

Therefore they say: "I seek refuge in God from the grip of the weak, for I am strong against the grip of the strong." When the weak gains the opportunity, he does not let it pass, because he cannot guarantee it at every time. As for the strong, he is confident in his strength and can overcome his opponent at any time. Hence the poet said:

"The weak one, when she hits an opportunity,
kills, just as the power of the weak is."

Therefore they have taken as evidence for the weakness of women His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your scheming is great.﴾ (12:28) Since their scheming is great, their weakness is also great, or even greater.

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And We made them the greatest losers.﴾ (21:70) The word "the greatest losers" (al-akhsarin) is the plural of akhsar, on the pattern af'al, to indicate intensification in loss. Their loss in the matter of Abraham's burning was of several aspects: first, Abraham, peace be upon him, was not harmed despite being thrown into the fire; then, they were not spared from his enmity; and after that, they will be requited for their deed in the Hereafter. This is in the Hereafter. So what loss is greater than this?

﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.﴾ (71)

﴿We delivered him...﴾ (al-Anbiya'): That is, there was harm that was going to reach him and injury that was going to befall him, and God delivered him from it. This deliverance was ongoing. After God had delivered him from the fire, He also delivered him from what he was exposed to from their harm.

﴿And Lot...﴾ (al-Anbiya'): Lot, peace be upon him, was the son of Ibrahim's brother. ﴿to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds﴾ (al-Anbiya'): That is, We said to Ibrahim: Leave this land, which is the land of Babylon in Iraq, and go to the holy land in al-Sham (Greater Syria), and take with you your brother's son. After God had delivered the two of them, He did not leave them in that place, but chose for them this holy place.

When the word "land" (ard) is qualified, it refers to a specific, particular land. When it is not qualified, it is used for the land in general, unless the context of the situation specifies it. For example, when Yusuf's brother said: ﴿So I will not leave the land until my father permits me...﴾ (Yusuf, 80), the context makes clear to us that it is the land of Egypt.

But His saying: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land...﴾ (al-Isra', 104) is not specified. This indicates that it is the land in general: dwell in the whole earth. That is, you will be scattered throughout it, and you will not have an independent homeland, as He said in another verse: ﴿And We divided them into communities upon the earth...﴾ (al-A'raf, 168).

Then, when God wills their gathering from dispersion: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes...﴾ (al-Isra', 104), that is, the time in which they will be victorious, ﴿We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude﾿ (al-Isra', 104). Thus they will gather in one place, and it will be easy to destroy them.

As for the meaning of ﴿which We had blessed therein...﴾ (al-Anbiya', 71): blessing (barakah) may be material or immaterial. The material blessing is the crops, fruits, rivers and goods. The immaterial blessing is the blessing of values in the holy land, which is the land of the prophets and the landmarks of prophethood and the messages.

Then the Truthful Lord says: ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.﴾

Here the Almighty gives us a snapshot from the story of Abraham, but one that is distant from the subject we are discussing. God granted Abraham Isaac when he supplicated God, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ (al-Saffat: 100). Although he already had Ishmael, Ishmael was from Hagar, and feelings of jealousy stirred in Sarah. She found in herself what women find regarding the matter of children, and [she wondered] how Abraham could have a son from Hagar, whom she herself had given to him in marriage, without her having a son like him.

Therefore Sarah insisted that Abraham ask God to grant her a child. Abraham prayed to his Lord, and the Almighty willed to answer Abraham and fulfil for him what his wife hoped for. But He wanted to give him this son in a doctrinal context that would be recorded and never fade from minds, and the son would remain linked to the event.

The beginning of the story of Isaac is when God commanded His prophet Abraham in a dream to slaughter his son Ishmael, so he informed him of his vision: ﴿O my son, I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so consider what you see...﴾ (al-Saffat: 102).

Abraham wanted to make his son a partner with him in this trial, and not to take him by surprise, lest his soul change toward his father and he come to hate him while not knowing what had happened. He also wanted not to deprive his son of the reward and recompense for this act of obedience and this patience in the face of trial.

As for Ishmael, on his part he did not object, nor did he say, for instance: "O father, this is merely a dream and not revelation; how can we build upon it?" Rather, we see him saying: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded...﴾ (al-Saffat: 102). He did not say, "Do what you say," for as long as the command is from God, do what you have been commanded: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ (al-Saffat: 102).

﴿So when they both had submitted...﴾ (al-Saffat: 103): that is, both of them, Abraham and Ishmael, ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ (al-Saffat: 103). It is said: "tallahu" means he placed his head upon the hill (tall), which is the elevated place of the ground. And ﴿upon his forehead﴾ (al-Saffat: 103) means he placed his brow directly upon the ground, such that he would slaughter him from the nape of the neck, and this is the swift and fruitful slaughter.

﴿And We called to him: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision..."﴾ (al-Saffat: 104–105). Since you have fulfilled the vision, there is a reward for good-doing for you; for you hastened to execute it although it was a dream. He could have delayed its execution, but as soon as the command came, his son carried it out.

So, the Almighty does not desire from His servant anything but that he submit to His decree. The one who said it spoke truly:

Submit to your Lord's judgment, for He decrees with wisdom,
so you may find rest and be at ease.
And mention the Friend of God in the slaughter of his son,
when his Creator spoke, and they both submitted.

Therefore God does not lift a decree He has issued upon His creatures unless He is pleased with it, and no one compels God to anything. We give, for this, an example — and to God belongs the highest description — of a father who enters and finds his son doing something he dislikes, so he rebukes him or strikes him a light blow expressing his anger. If the son submits to his father and yields, the father returns tender and affectionate toward him, perhaps embracing him and reconciling with him. But if the son opposes and is insolent to his father, the father becomes harsher and multiplies the punishment for him, and his severity toward him increases.

And so it was with Abraham: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ (al-Saffat: 107). We ransomed Ishmael for him. Not only that, but ﴿We gave him the good news of Isaac...﴾ (al-Saffat: 112). Then He increased him by making Isaac also a prophet like Ishmael. This is the occasion for the discussion of Isaac and Jacob.

Here the Most High says: ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift...﴾ (al-Anbiya: 72). The "nafilah" (additional gift)¹ means increase. He had asked his Lord for a righteous offspring, so God gave him good news of Isaac, and after him Jacob, and all of them were prophets. Therefore He said "nafilah," meaning: something added beyond what you requested. The answer to the supplication was Isaac, and the increase was Jacob. A person's joy in his son is great, and in his grandson greater, as they say: "Dearer than a son is a son's son." A person secures the survival of his memory through his offspring, and if a grandson comes, he secures his memory for yet another generation.

The gift came from God, because the woman was not fit for childbearing, as indicated by the Most High's words: ﴿So his wife came forward in a cry (sarrah),² and she struck her face and said: "An old barren woman!"﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 29). He answered her: ﴿They said: "Do you wonder at the command of God?"﴾ (Hud: 73). That is, He is capable of all things.

The Truthful Lord says: ﴿And We made each of them righteous﴾ (al-Anbiya: 72). So the grandson is an additional gift and an increase in the bestowal of offspring, and an intensification of honour. Then God bestows favour upon all of them by making them righteous and making them prophets, as He said in another verse: ﴿And each of them We made a prophet﴾ (Maryam: 49).

¹ Nafilah: the grandson, because he is an increase after the son. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/280). Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4484): (That is, an increase; for he prayed for Isaac, and Jacob was added without a prayer, so that was a nafilah, that is, an addition to what was asked. And a son's son is called a nafilah because he is an addition to the son.)

² Sarrah: a cry (of astonishment), or a frowning of the face, or a company of her servants; that is, she came forward in a cry of wonder, or with a frowning face in disbelief and astonishment, or in a company of her attendants. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/374)

³ The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him.

⁴ Sakk: a hard strike with a broad object; it is said it is a general term for striking with anything. (Lisan al-Arab, root ṣ-k-k)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 73:

A'immah (imams): The meaning of imamah here is not temporal authority over people, but the imamah of exemplary guidance by God's command, ﴿guiding by Our command﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:73). They do not act in anything except upon guidance from God.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We inspired them to do good deeds﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:73). That is: He opens for them the doors of goodness and facilitates for them its circumstances, because the one granted success, who has readiness for goodness, God opens for him the channels of goodness and helps him to it.

﴿And to establish prayer and to give zakah﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:73). Establishing prayer is the very essence of all good deeds, because good deeds are a blessing, but establishing prayer is standing in the presence of the Bestower, glory be to Him. So prayer is the best of goods.

Yet we find someone who busies himself away from prayer, and makes excuses of work and lack of time, etc. All of these are feeble excuses. I used to say to some of these people: "By God, if you needed the lavatory, would you find time or not?" He says: "I would find the time." Then why do you contrive in this matter and arrange the necessary time, but do not contrive for the time of prayer?

Your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, if He knew that you would answer His call, would have made answering easy for you. We have seen that the Truthful, glory be to Him, subjects even the disbeliever to help you in the matter of prayer.

On one of our journeys to Belgium, we saw that the children of Muslims there were not taught anything of the Islamic religion in the schools; rather, they were taught the Christian religion. We requested a meeting with their Minister of Education and spoke with him on this matter. Our argument was: You accepted the presence of these Muslims in your country because of your need for them and their contribution to the movement of your life, and it is in your interest that these Muslims have a religion that monitors them before you monitor them. You are the first to benefit from teaching the Islamic religion to the children of Muslims.

And indeed, the next day they issued a decision to teach the Islamic religion in their schools to the children of Muslims. That is because Islam is a fruitful religion, a positive religion that you embrace and that secures you.

Because of the importance of prayer, the Truthful, glory be to Him, mentioned it first among the good deeds, and at their forefront. The summit of goods is to be in the presence of the God who bestows these goods upon you.

﴿And giving zakah﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:73). Zakah is the practical application of responding to God when you bring out a portion of your wealth for God. Prayer is always paired with zakah, so the relationship between them is strong. Zakah is a sacrifice of wealth, and wealth is in reality the result of work, and work is a branch of time; but prayer is a sacrifice of time itself.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they were worshippers of Us﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:73). That is: obedient to Our commands, avoiding Our prohibitions, for worship is the obedience of a worshipper to the one he worships.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 74:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We delivered him from the town which was committing the abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿And Lot..﴾ (al-Anbiya') : It is in the accusative because it is coordinated with the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment..﴾ (al-Anbiya', 51), and also: "We gave Lot his sound judgment." The word hukm means hikmah (wisdom), and its origin is from the hikmah (bit) that is placed in the horse's jaw, because the horse may bolt with its rider or head in a direction not intended by its rider. Therefore the bridle or the hikmah is placed on its jaw. The hikmah is a piece of iron with two ends, by which the horse is steered to the right or to the left.

From this comes hikmah, which is placing a thing in its proper place. From it also comes hukm, which is placing the right in its proper place between the complainant and the complained against, i.e., the two disputants.

﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge..﴾ (al-Anbiya', 74): There is a difference between 'ilm (knowledge) and hukm (judgment). 'Ilm is that you verify and recognize; hukm, however, is conduct and application of what you know. So 'ilm is verification and hukm is application.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And We delivered him from the town which was committing the abominations..﴾ (al-Anbiya', 74): God saved Abraham, peace be upon him, from the fire, and likewise saved Lot from the people of the town which was committing the abominations. The abominations among the people of Lot are well known, so after it He says: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ (al-Anbiya', 74). A man of evil (rajul al-su') is one who harms everyone who associates with him; he does not harm some and not others. Everyone who mixes with him or comes into contact with him is harmed by him.

And fisq (defiant disobedience) is going out of the commands of obligation. This expression, like all Qur'anic expressions, is drawn from the realities of life among the Arabs. The root of fisq is from "fasaqat al-rutabah 'an qishratiha" (the date pulled out of its skin), when the unripe date ripens and its skin separates from it until the date appears. This skin was made to perform a task, which is preserving the fruit. Likewise we say about fisq from the religious method which came to perform a task in our lives: whoever goes out from it is a fāsiq.

1 It is the town of (Sodom). Ibn 'Abbas said: there were seven towns; Gabriel, peace be upon him, overturned six and left one for Lot and his family, which is Zughar, in which there are fruits, from the district of Palestine to the border of the Sarat, and it has many villages up to the border of the Red Sea. Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4484).
2 al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4485): ("Regarding the abominations they used to commit there are two opinions: one: sodomy (liwat). The second: breaking wind (dara), i.e., they used to break wind in their gatherings and assemblies.").
3 Hikmah: an iron piece in the bridle that is placed on the horse's nose and jaw, preventing it from disobeying its rider. (Lisan al-'Arab, root h-k-m).
4 Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "There were ten characteristics among the people of Lot by which they were known: pigeon-racing, throwing the bunduq (pellets), whistling (mukā', whistling with the mouth), pebble-flicking at the gatherings (khadhf fi al-andiya', throwing pebbles or date stones), combing hair in a particular way (tasbīt al-sha'r), cracking chewing gum (faq'at al-'alak, the lubān), letting the izar trail (isbāl al-izar, lengthening it beyond the ankles), confining the cloaks (ḥabs al-aqbiyah), sexual intercourse with men (ityān al-rajul), and drinking companionship over wine, and this nation will add to it." (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 5/644).

Then the Truthful Lord says: ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed, he was among the righteous.﴾ (21:75)

How? Are we not all within the mercy of Allah? They said: Because there is a general mercy for all creation, which encompasses even the disbeliever, and there is a special mercy whose benefit extends from the one who receives it to others. By this they mean prophethood, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?"﴾ (43:31). So Allah responded to them: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ (43:32), that is, prophethood: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world...﴾ (43:32).

So how could they distribute the mercy of Allah, which is prophethood, and which is the pinnacle of their lives, while We distribute to them their provisions and livelihoods in this world?

Thus the meaning of ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy...﴾ (21:75) is: into the company of prophethood. ﴿Indeed, he was among the righteous﴾ (21:75): that is, fit for prophethood. And Allah knows best where He places His message. But the pinnacle of this mercy came in the Final Prophet and the Messenger after whom there is no other messenger; therefore his Lord addressed him, saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ (21:107).

So the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) were a mercy to their own peoples, but Muhammad (ﷺ) is a mercy to all the worlds.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, tells us about another messenger from among the Messengers of firm resolve:

And Noah, when he called out before; so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress. (76)

The Almighty's words, "And Noah... (76)" (al-Anbiya'), are like what we said regarding "And Lot... (74)" (al-Anbiya'): that is, We gave him, too, his right guidance. "When he called out before, so We responded to him..." (76) (al-Anbiya'): The nida' (calling out), in its reality, is a request for attention. If it is from a higher to a lower, it is nida'; if it is from an equal to you, it is iltimas (entreaty); and if it is from a lower to a higher, it is du'a' (supplication). So when you say "Ya Rabb" (O Lord), the ya' here is not for nida' but for du'a'.

When you test a student and say to him, "Parse: rabbi ighfir li" (My Lord, forgive me), if he were intelligent he would say: "Rabb is a mad'u (one being supplicated)," and the estimate is "ya Rabb." Whoever says "munada" (vocative) we excuse him, because it is also correct; the ya' in its origin is for nida', but it is imprecise in its performance. Likewise with "ighfir li": if he says it is a verb in the imperative, we give him half the grade; but if he says it is a du'a', he has the full grade.

So what did Noah, peace be upon him, say in his calling out? What is meant is his saying: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers any dwellers (1)" (Nuh, 26). So God responded to His Prophet Noah, peace be upon him: "So We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress (76)" (al-Anbiya'). The distress meant is what Noah endured in calling his people, over a span of time that extended a thousand years less fifty years, and what he bore in the cause of his call of hardship and difficulty, of which God said:

"And indeed, every time I have called them that You may forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments and persisted and became arrogantly proud. Then I invited them openly. Then I announced to them and confided to them secretly. (7-9)" (Nuh).

Then, when God commanded him to build the ship, they began to mock him: "And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a company of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him... (38)" (Hud).

Thus: God responded to his supplication and his calling out, "so We responded to him... (76)" (al-Anbiya'), and in another place: "And Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best of responders (75)" (al-Saffat).

So the Truth, glory be to Him, described His response to Noah with "ni'ma" (the best of), which indicates praise.

Does that mean there is someone who would be "bi'sa al-mujib" (the worst of responders)? They said: Yes, if you ask someone for something and he grants it to you while it is evil for you. As for the Truth, glory be to Him, He is the best of responders, because He never responds to you except with what is good and beneficial for you; if your supplication contains evil, He turns it away, knowing, glory be to Him, that it will not benefit you.

It is as if the Supreme Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to you: "I am not an employee of yours; I respond to you in everything you ask. Rather, I am the Guardian over you. You may supplicate for what you think is good for you, while I, by the eternity of My knowledge, know that it is an evil with no good in it; so the good for you is that I do not respond to you, for I am the best of responders."

Suppose God responded to each of us with what he wants: how would it be with a mother who, for example, becomes angry with her only son and, in a moment of anger and fury, invokes a curse upon him, saying, for instance: "My God, let your fire drink him"? The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, when He rejects such a supplication, is the best of responders, because He is the best of withholders.

Therefore He, exalted is He, says: "And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good; and man has always been hasty (11)" (al-Isra'). That is: he calls and insists in supplication for what he thinks is good, while it is not so.

(1) al-Diyar: one who inhabits the house, or one who moves and roams in it freely. It is said: "ma bil-dar diyar," meaning there is no one in it. The meaning of Noah's supplication, peace be upon him, is: do not leave any of them alive. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/237).
(2) Istaghsha thiyabahu and taghasha biha: he covered himself with them so as not to see or hear. (Lisan al-Arab, root gh-sh-y).

The verses still relate to us a brief portion from the caravan of prophets, and we are in Surah al-Anbiya' (The Prophets). When we reflect on this verse, we find that Allah, exalted is He, punishes with water just as He punishes with fire, even though the two are opposites that do not meet. None can bring about this matter except their Creator, glory be to Him.

The story of the drowning of the people of Noah and the people of Sheba after the collapse of the Marib Dam created a complex among the people of the Arabian Peninsula. So when they see water, they fear it and keep away from it, and even when they need water they go to a distant place to fill their waterskins. That is because of their awareness of the danger of the deluge, and that nothing can repel it or turn it back from them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 78:

Then Allah, glory be to Him, tells us about two prophets from among the prophets of the Children of Israel, after Moses:

﴿And [remember] Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field, when the flock of certain people had strayed into it by night, and We were witness to their judgement.﴾
