"Yahkumani" (they two were judging) means that there was a dispute between two parties. "Al-harth" (the tilled field): the stirring up of the land and the turning over of the soil so that it becomes fit for cultivation. The word "harth" also occurs in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He destroys the crop and the progeny﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:205).

The tilled land itself is not destroyed; what is destroyed is the crops and fruits that grow from it. So the crop was called "harth" because it arises from it, as in His saying, exalted is He, also: ﴿Like a wind containing a freezing cold that strikes the tilled field of a people who have wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:117).

But why was the tilled land called "zar'" (crop), when "harth" is merely the preparation of the land for cultivation? They said: to make clear that there is no planting except with tilling, because tilling is the loosening of the soil's surface. This process helps air enter the soil and dries it of excess water, because after repeated irrigation a sticky layer forms on the land that blocks the soil's pores and prevents the evaporation of the groundwater, which causes harm to the roots of the plant.

Therefore, it is not a mark of good soil that it be purely clay or purely sand: clay soil holds water, and sandy soil lets water seep away, and both are unsuitable for plants. Good soil, however, is that which combines these two, so that it allows the plant the necessary aeration and gives it water in proportion to its need.

Therefore the crop was called "harth," because it is the cause of its growth, its increase and its quality, and to draw our attention that there is no crop without tilling, as came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered what you plough? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ (al-Waqi'ah 56:63-64).

In this matter there is an indication of one of Allah's laws in the cosmos: that you must work in order to attain. Your Lord and Creator bestowed His bounty upon you even before you existed, and before He charged you with anything, and you remained until the age of puberty taking from Allah's bounty without being held to account for any of your conduct.

Likewise in the Hereafter He will give you a bounty that does not end, without your having to exert yourself in seeking it; all of this is in return for your obedience to Him in voluntary matters during the age of responsibility.

So: you received before you worked, and you will receive in the Hereafter likewise without working; yet you must work between your beginning and your end in order to attain the fruit.

Therefore, in the noble hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Give the hired worker his wage before his sweat dries," since once he has worked he has earned the wage, and the matter of tilling is the same.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿When the flock of certain people had strayed into it by night...﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:78). This was a dispute between two parties, who brought their case before Dawud, peace be upon him: a man had a crop, and another had a flock. The flock wandered off while its owner was heedless, and ate the crop. The owner of the crop complained to the owner of the flock to Dawud, and he judged in this case that the owner of the crop should take the flock, and perhaps Sayyidina Dawud found that the crop destroyed by the flock was equal in value to it.

When the two disputants went out, Sulayman, peace be upon him, met them. He was eleven years old, and he learned from them the judgement of his father in this case, and he said: "A different ruling would be gentler to both parties." He called his father's judgement "gentleness" and did not accuse him of injustice, for example, but he had something gentler.

When his words reached his father, he asked him: "What is the gentler ruling for both parties?" Sulayman said: "We give the flock to the owner of the crop, to benefit from its milk and wool, and we give the land to the owner of the flock to restore it until it returns to how it was. At that time the owner of the flock takes his flock and the owner of the crop takes his crop."

The meaning of ﴿nafashat﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:78): we say "nafasha al-shay'," meaning it took on a size greater than its size, as when you take, for example, a piece of bread or rusk and place it in milk or water; you notice that it swells and its size increases. We say "intafasha" (it swelled), just as we say to someone who takes on a greater size than his own: "You are puffing up your feathers."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We were witness to their judgement﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:78): that is, watching over them.

¹ Al-nafsh: grazing by night. "Nafashat": that is, it grazed in it by night. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4475).
"Nafashat al-ibil" means when camels scattered and grazed at night without the knowledge of their herder. (Lisan al-'Arab, entry: nafash.)
² Al-sirr: intense cold (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/374). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (1/397): "(From Ibn 'Abbas also and Mujahid: 'fiha sirr') meaning fire, and this returns to the first, for intense cold, especially frost, burns crops and fruits just as fire burns things."
³ Narrated by Abu Nu'aym in Hilyat al-Awliya' (7/142) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah; al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Saghir (1/20) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (2443) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. Two weak narrators are in the chain of Ibn Majah, as stated by al-Busiri in al-Zawa'id.
⁴ Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (6/4478) that Sulayman asked the two disputants after they had left his father Dawud: "By what did the prophet of Allah Dawud judge between you?" They said: "With the flock to the owner of the tilled field." He said: "Perhaps the ruling is other than this; come with me." He went to his father and said: "O prophet of Allah, you judged with such-and-such, and I saw what is gentler to all." He stated his judgement between the two disputants. Dawud said: "You have been granted success, my son; may Allah not cut off your understanding."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 21, verse 79:

The Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says: ﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Solomon, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with David, and the birds [too]. And We were the Doers.﴾

David and Solomon, peace be upon them, were both prophets, each with his own station. God gave them both judgement and knowledge, yet their opinions differed on this matter. What Solomon arrived at does not detract from David's knowledge, nor does it cast doubt on his judgement.

The judgements of David and Solomon may be likened to a court of first instance, a court of second instance, a court of cassation, and a court of appeal. Beware of thinking that when a court of appeal overturns the ruling of a court of first instance, it is impugning it.

This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Solomon...﴾ (al-Anbiya'). He gave a ruling different from that of his father. Thus the primary judge may rule on a case, and the matter is deferred until it is elevated to a judge of appeal, who reads the same case with another perspective, so his ruling differs from the first.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with David, and the birds...﴾ (al-Anbiya'). When the Qur'anic context joins David and Solomon, it intends to show us a portion of what God bestowed upon them. His saying, ﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Solomon...﴾ (al-Anbiya'), is a manifestation of his distinction, and here He shows a feature of David, peace be upon him: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with David, and the birds...﴾ (al-Anbiya').

Taskhir (subjugation) is the compelling of the subjugated to an act from which it cannot separate itself, and in which it has no choice. We notice here an ascent from the lower to the higher: first, He subjected the mountains, which are inanimate; then the birds, which are higher than the inanimate. But if we conceive of glorification from the birds, because they are living, possessed of a soul, of movement and of expressive sound, how could glorification come from the silent mountains?

Some scholars, when they encounter this verse, take it at its outward meaning, without depth or reflection on the essence of things. They regard the mountains as solid, without an expressive voice as birds have, and so they marvel at the saying that the mountains glorify. How could they do so, being inanimate?

But what is strange about that? If you were to make a comprehensive survey of the races of mankind on earth, and of the variety of their languages, tongues, forms and colours according to the environments in which they live, you would find that people differ in such matters and agree only in their instincts. Hunger, thirst, fear, laughter and emotions are all instincts shared by all races, and these shared instincts involve no choice.

Have you not considered His saying: ﴿And that it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep.﴾ (al-Najm, 43)?

Since it is He who makes [people] laugh and weep, we will not differ over these matters.

Speech, then, is among the things on which people differ, and this difference is not in the sound of the letters, for the letters are the same. For example, when we pronounce (Sharshal), people of other languages pronounce it likewise: shin after shin and lam; so we are united in the letters, but we differ in the meanings of things.

Some throats find it difficult to pronounce certain letters due to their natural formation. The non-Arab, for instance, does not pronounce the ḍād; they have only the dāl. In Arabic, however, there is a distinction between the light dāl and the emphatic ḍād, a distinction between sīn and thā', between zāy and dhāl, and between hamzah and ʿayn. Thus you find the non-Arab saying "ʿalā" as "alay": he lacks the ability to pronounce the ʿayn, though he is a human being who speaks a language and talks.

If we, human beings, do not understand each other's languages, this one is Arab, that one English, another French, and so on, then if you do not learn that language, you will not understand it.

It is well known that language is the daughter of imitation and the daughter of hearing: what the ear hears, the tongue reproduces. The mute who does not speak is one who cannot hear, and the child speaks what he hears. So if an English child were placed in an Arab environment, he would speak Arabic, and so on.

So why are we surprised when we do not understand the language of the birds or the language of inanimate things, which are entirely different from us? Our failure to understand their languages does not mean that they have no language among themselves, by which they know one another and express themselves.

Therefore, do not rule out that the lower kinds than you have languages by which they understand one another, and which you do not understand. The evidence is that God gave us a glimpse of the languages of the birds, and that is known only to whom God has taught it, just as God favoured Solomon and taught him the language of the birds, so he understood them and addressed them.

The Truthful, glory be to Him, related of him: ﴿O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of all things...﴾ (al-Naml, 16). Had God not taught him the language of the birds, he would not have known it.

And here is the hoopoe saying to Solomon, peace be upon him, when he inspected the birds and did not find the hoopoe, and threatened it: ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news.﴾ (al-Naml, 22).

Here we notice Solomon's, peace be upon him, precision in reviewing his kingdom: he left nothing out, not even the hoopoe. And we notice his courtesy in his saying: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?﴾ (al-Naml, 20): he first doubted his own sight and suspected himself, for perhaps the hoopoe was present and Solomon had not seen it.

Look at the hoopoe's words to the king: ﴿I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed...﴾ (al-Naml, 22), then his precise knowledge of the matter of monotheism and creed: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God...﴾ (al-Naml, 24).

The hoopoe objects to this polytheism and responds with something specific to himself, a matter that concerns him: ﴿Why do they not prostrate to God, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth...﴾ (al-Naml, 25).

The hoopoe chose the matter of bringing forth what is hidden (al-khabʾ) because his food comes from it: he does not eat from the surface of the earth, but must dig into the ground and bring out what is hidden in order to eat it.

Likewise the ant, which is smaller than the hoopoe: an ant had a language and speech with Solomon, and he understood her: ﴿When they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive." So he smiled, laughing at her saying...﴾ (al-Naml, 18-19).

So the speech was the ant's, but Solomon understood it; therefore he said: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be thankful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me...﴾ (al-Naml, 19).

That is because we do not understand these languages unless God gives us understanding of them.

Yet when the scholars stood before this verse, ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with David...﴾ (al-Anbiya', 79), they said: the glorification here means glorification by indication (dalalah): the mountains, in their state, point to the Creator, exalted is He, and the intended meaning is not glorification in its literal sense. It would have been more fitting for them to acknowledge the mountains' glorification, but it is a glorification we do not understand, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But you do not understand their glorification...﴾ (al-Isra', 44).

Nowadays we see the aspirations of scientists to compile a dictionary of the language of fish and the language of some animals, and we do not rule out that in the future a dictionary of the language of stones and inanimate things will be compiled. Otherwise, how will the advancement of science proceed in the future? This is a truth the Qur'an has already established, awaiting modern science to discover it.

The distinction God granted to His prophet David, peace be upon him, does not lie in the glorification of the mountains, since the mountains glorify with him and with others. Rather, the distinction lies in that they echo him, and respond to him in glorification: when David says, "Glory be to God," the mountains repeat after him, "Glory be to God," as though they are all a chorus repeating a single hymn.

Inanimacy does not mean that a thing has no life. It is inanimate in terms of its form of composition, but if you reflect on the quarries in the layers of the earth, you will find among the stones life, interaction and movement for millions of years. As a result of this movement the colour of a stone changes and its nature changes, and this is evidence of life in it. Look, for example, if you paint a room a certain colour, you see it change with the passage of time. So there is life in these inanimate things, but we do not perceive it.

We have already pointed out that those who say, regarding the miracles of the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he glorified the pebbles in his hand, this statement is not precise and needs rational refinement: the stone glorifies in the hand of the Messenger of God, and in the hand of Abu Jahl. So say: the miracle is that the Messenger of God heard the pebbles glorifying in his hand.

There is nothing in God's creation that does not have a life suited to it, and a language by which it glorifies God, whether we have perceived it or not, because speech is a branch of the existence of life, and everything in existence has life. This matchbox we use, the scientists say, has among its particles interactions sufficient to run a train around the world. These interactions are evidence of movement and life.

Has not the Truthful, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face...﴾ (al-Qasas, 88)?

Everything that is called a thing, except the Face of God, is perishing, and perishing means that it has life, for perishing is the opposite of life, as He said: ﴿That whoever perishes might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives might live upon clear proof﴾ (al-Anfal, 42).

Everything in existence has life according to its law. It is not necessary that you hear speech before you acknowledge its existence. There is, for example, the language of signs, which is an understood and expressive language. Do you not see the servant who looks at his master with a mere glance, from which he understands what he is to bring to the guest, for example?

Sailors have signals by which they know one another and communicate. The telegraph is a kind of expression and a means of communication. So expression and clarity do not necessarily take place through audible speech; peoples communicate and speak to one another, each in its own language. If God wishes to bestow upon you of His illuminations, He gives you insight and knowledge by which you understand the languages of other kinds.

Therefore He says: ﴿Each has known its prayer and its glorification...﴾ (al-Nur, 41). The tanwin here indicates generality: for every thing there is its prayer that suits it, and its glorification that suits its nature.

When the Truthful, glory be to Him, presents the matter of glorification, submission and subjugation to Him by all creatures, the speech comes in general terms covering all kinds without exception, except when speaking of man, for glorification and submission then pertain to some people only.

Read His saying: ﴿Have you not seen that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the beasts...﴾ (al-Hajj, 18). Thus, without exception. But of man He says: ﴿And many of mankind, and many deserve the punishment. And whoever God humiliates, for him there is no honourer. Indeed, God does what He wills.﴾ (al-Hajj, 18).

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We were the Doers.﴾ (al-Anbiya', 79). Yes, the Truthful, glory be to Him, is the Creator of every thing and the Doer of every thing. Yet He affirms this truth so that we do not wonder at the glorification of birds and inanimate things: God is the Doer, the Giver and the Mover.

1 Al-khabʾ: that which is hidden, concealed. (al-Qamus al-qawim 1/185). It has been said: the khabʾ in the heavens is rain, and the khabʾ in the earth is plants. It has been said: the sounder view is that khabʾ is everything that is hidden. (Lisan al-'Arab, root: kh-b-ʾ).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 80:

Then the Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says about Dawud (peace be upon him): ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence. Will you then be grateful?﴾

﴿"We taught him..." (80)﴾ (al-Anbiya): Knowledge ('ilm) is the transmission of a beneficial matter in existence from one who knows it to one who does not. Man is always in need of knowledge and learning, because he is the vicegerent of God on earth, and he will not fulfil this mission except through wide movement among people. This movement requires understanding, knowledge, interaction, and the exchange of knowledge and cultures. For example, shaping iron requires heating it until it becomes soft and malleable, and water must be boiled for such-and-such, and so on.

The matters of knowledge that human movement on earth requires are of two kinds. The first is a kind in which God did not entrust creatures with their own selves, so He brought it through revelation, so that reason has no room in it and desires and passions do not disagree about it. This is the method that came down saying to you: do such-and-such, and do not do such-and-such.

But there are matters on which desires do not disagree, rather they strive to meet upon them and race towards them, and some may even steal from others. These matters God, glory be to Him, left to the work of minds and their aspirations, and they may be inspired through a thought or through learning, even from the lowest source, as the son of Adam (Qabil) learned from the crow how to cover the nakedness of his brother. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to cover the nakedness of his brother...﴾ (31) (al-Ma'ida).

A scientific matter may have precursors in the cosmos when we employ the intellect and relate some phenomena to others, arriving from them at scientific truths. A scientific matter may come through experiment, or through a thought that God casts into the heart of a person.

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you...﴾ (80) (al-Anbiya): it is valid to say that this teaching was through revelation, or through experiment, or through inspiration cast into the mind. This craft was not known before Dawud (peace be upon him).

Al-Lubus (the coat of mail) is more eloquent and more precise than al-libas (clothing). Al-libas, from the same root (l-b-s), is the garments that cover the human's nakedness and protect him from heat and cold, as came in His saying: ﴿And He made for you garments (sarabil) to protect you from the heat...﴾ (81) (al-Nahl).

As for war, we need greater protection and more defence than the ordinary kind found in clothing. In war we need what safeguards us from violence and protects us from the enemy's blows in the deadly places. Therefore people were guided to making the helmet and the shield to protect the dangerous places of the human body, which are represented in the head and the chest. In the head is the brain, and in the chest is the heart. If these organs are safe, then whatever is below them can be treated and mended.

Therefore: al-lubus is more eloquent and more protective than al-libas, because its function is more eloquent than the function of clothing. This was the craft of Dawud (peace be upon him): he would make shields. Before Dawud the shield was smooth, so the sword would slide off it; when Dawud made it, he made it of interlocking rings so that the sword would break upon it. Therefore after it He said, exalted is He: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾ (80) (al-Anbiya): that is, to shield you in your war with your enemy, and to prevent you and surround you.

Therefore: We inspired Dawud (peace be upon him), and he began to think and innovate. Every thinking towards advancing a craft arises from noticing a defect in a previous craft, so the later one tries to avoid the errors of the earlier, and so on until we reach something without defect, or at least one that avoids the defects of its predecessor. Therefore they call it "the latest model."

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ (80) (al-Anbiya): grateful for the blessing of God who watches over you and protects you in predicaments and difficult situations. He, glory be to Him, chose the situation of violence before the enemy, to give us a sign of the necessity of preparing the believer to confront the disbeliever, and of taking the means of salvation if confrontation occurs.

In another verse He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great violence and benefits for people, and that God may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed God is Strong and Mighty.﴾ (25) (al-Hadid).

So the function of iron in life is not merely that it benefits people; it also has a combative function. Therefore He said: ﴿And We sent down iron...﴾ (25) (al-Hadid), just as He said: ﴿We sent down upon you the Qur'an...﴾ (23) (al-Insan). If the Qur'an is for guidance, then iron supports this guidance, for with it we strike the hands of the disbelieving rebels, and with it we protect the chests of the believing faithful. Therefore He said ﴿We sent down...﴾ (25) (al-Hadid): that is, from above, although it comes out of the earth.

Therefore: the matter of iron on earth is a great blessing from God upon us, by which we protect ourselves from the enemy. God, glory be to Him and exalted, created creation and did not leave it to manage its affairs as it is; rather He created it and set for it a law of its protection and preservation. This deserves from us constant gratitude that does not cease.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4500): "The craft keeps a person from relying on people, and by it he repels harm and violence from himself. In the hadith: 'God loves the believing, self-supporting, modest tradesman, and hates the importunate beggar who presses.' The craft of Dawud was the making of shields."

2 Al-sirbal: the shirt and the coat of mail. It is said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿sarabil that protect you from the heat...﴾ (81) (al-Nahl): these are shirts that protect from heat and cold, and He mentioned only the heat, as if what protects from heat protects from cold too. As for His saying: ﴿and sarabil that protect you from your violence...﴾ (81) (al-Nahl), these are coats of mail (Lisan al-'Arab, root: s-r-b-l).

3 Qatada said: they were plates; the first to stretch and link them was Dawud (peace be upon him). Reported by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/650) and attributed by him to 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama.

Then the context moves from speaking of Dawud to his son Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and the Truthful, Glorified One says: ﴿And to Sulayman (We subjected) the wind, violent, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed; and We are ever Knowing of all things.﴾

There is no doubt that Sulayman, peace be upon him, benefited from what Allah had taught his father Dawud, and took from the blessing of Allah upon his father. Here his Lord, blessed and exalted, grants him further matters that distinguish him, among them the violent wind, that is, the strong and powerful one: ﴿running by his command toward the land which We had blessed﴾ (al-Anbiya'). It was as if it were internal transport within his kingdom, from Iraq to Palestine.(1)

In another place He says: ﴿"My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me; indeed, You are the Bestower." So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently by his command wherever he intended﴾ (Sad).

Gently (rakhā'): that is, mild, soft and smooth. Here He said: ﴿violent﴾ (al-Anbiya'). So it is as if Allah combined for this wind the quality of speed in "violent" and the quality of comfort in "gentle", and these are two qualities that no one can combine except Allah. When a car, for example, speeds us along, the quality of comfort and reassurance is not available to us; rather, people become frightened and ask for the speed to be reduced.

As for Sulayman's wind, it carried him swiftly to his desired destination, and at the same time it was soothing, smooth and calm, not affecting the make-up of his body, nor causing him any jolt or thrust of force that would require, for example, a safety belt. Who can combine these qualities except Allah, the Restrainer, the Expander, who contracts time for some people and expands it for others?

The meaning of ﴿which We had blessed﴾ (al-Anbiya'): that is, a tangible blessing, through what is in it of crops, fruits, fertility and good things, and a spiritual blessing, in that He made it the place of the descent of revelation and prophethood and the traces of the prophets.

The subjugation of the wind to Sulayman does not mean that it carried him, for example, as we saw in the cinema, the flying carpet that we see carrying something and moving it through the air, nor that it propelled ships in the seas. Rather, what is meant by its subjugation to him is that it be under his command and obey his order, moving wherever he wills, to the right or to the left. It does not blow according to the natural tendencies that Allah created it with, but according to his own will.

And if this gentle wind carried him on an internal journey within his kingdom, there are also winds that carry him on external journeys and voyages, like what Allah the Exalted said about it: ﴿And to Sulayman (We subjected) the wind: its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ (Saba'). So he traverses the universe with it as he wills ﴿wherever he intended﴾ (Sad).

Then the Exalted says: ﴿and We are ever Knowing of all things﴾ (al-Anbiya'). That is, with Us is knowledge by which We arrange affairs in accordance with Our will, and We break for Our will the law of things, so We move the wind as We love, not as nature requires.

(1) Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He would set out in the morning on his carpet from Damascus and land at Istakhr for his midday meal, then depart from Istakhr in the afternoon and spend the night at Kabul; between Damascus and Istakhr is a full month for a swift traveller, and between Istakhr and Kabul is a full month for a swift traveller. Transmitted by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/528). Kabul is now the capital of Afghanistan.

Then the Truthful One (subhanahu) says: ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him and did work other than that, and We were guardians over them.﴾

After Allah subjected the wind to him, He subjected the devils to him: ﴿who dived for him...﴾ (al-Anbiya). Al-ghawS (diving) is descending into the depths of the sea, to bring him its treasures, its precious things and its wonders which Allah has stored in it. ﴿and did work other than that...﴾ (al-Anbiya): that is, of the arduous tasks which Sulayman assigned them, which a human being cannot perform. This verse has been explained in another place: ﴿They made for him what he willed of arches, statues, bowls like water-troughs (al-jawab), and fixed cooking-pots.﴾ (Saba' 13). Thus he included the various kinds of work within His will.

Al-mahareeb (sing. mihrab) is the plural of mihrab, which is a place of worship, like the qiblah for example. Al-jifan (sing. jafnah) is a large, wide bowl that suffices a great number of people. Al-qudur al-rasiyat means those that are fixed, which are not moved from place to place, being built.

We have seen something of this in Riyadh in the days of King Abd al-Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him: such a pot was of a size and height that when a person stood stretching his arms upward, they did not reach its height. In the pre-Islamic era such pots were famous with Ibn Jud'an and with Mut'im ibn 'Adi.

As for statues (tamathil), they are well known, and the position on them has been clear since the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he broke them and forbade their worship. This refutes the view of those who say that statues were permissible, and then people were tempted by them and worshipped them besides Allah, so they were prohibited. So how do we get out of this position? And how does Allah bestow favour upon His prophet Sulayman by subjecting to him those who make statues, when they are forbidden?

We say: they made statues for him not for the purpose of glorification and worship, but in the form of humiliation and belittlement, such as making them in the form of a mighty man, or a huge lion carrying a part of the palace or one of its balconies, or depicting them carrying a dining table, etc. That is, they were not by way of sanctification.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿and We were guardians over them﴾ (al-Anbiya): guardians over the people contemporary with these works, so that the devils do not harm them or frighten them. It is known that the devils see humans while humans do not see them, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them.﴾ (al-A'raf 27).

As for Sulayman (peace be upon him), he could see the jinn and watch them while they worked for him. In his story: ﴿So when We decreed death for him, nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth eating his staff (minsa'atahu).﴾ (Saba' 14). In this is evidence that the jinn do not know the unseen; therefore Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when he fell, the jinn realised that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾ (Saba' 14).

It is said that Sulayman (peace be upon him), after Allah had bestowed favour upon him and given him a kingdom that should not belong to anyone after him, took these jinn and confined them in qama'im (vessels) so that they would not work for anyone other than him.

This is merely a glimpse from the story of Sulayman.

Footnote 1: al-jawab: plural of jabiyah, which is the basin in which water is collected; Ibn 'Abbas said: like cisterns (al-hiyad). Likewise said Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/528)

Footnote 2: al-minsa'ah: the thick staff, in the Abyssinian tongue. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/262)

The narrative now moves from them to Ayyub (peace be upon him):

﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ (21:83)

(nādā): We have said that "nidā'" (calling out) directed to someone like you implies seeking attention, but when it concerns Allah, the Exalted, it carries the sense of supplication (du'ā'). So the meaning of ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ (21:83) is: he supplicated to Him and called upon Him with a request, namely ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ (21:83). And ḍurr (adversity), with a ḍammah on the ḍād, is a trial from Allah in his body, by sickness or something else.

As for ḍarr (with a fatḥah on the ḍād), it is harm and trial in anything other than the body. There is no objection to prophets becoming ill with an illness that does not repel people.

But how could Ayyub (peace be upon him) call out to his Lord and complain, saying ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me"﴾ (21:83)? Does not Allah know that adversity had touched Ayyub? And is it fitting for a prophet to complain about Allah's trial?

Yes, it is permissible for him to complain, because a servant does not show boldness toward his Lord. Thus, when a man entered upon Imam ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) to visit him while he was suffering from his illness and complaining, he said to him: "Do you complain, though you are Abu al-Ḥasan?" He replied: "I am not bold before Allah," meaning: "I am not a champion before Allah."

Do you not see that, in courtesy toward someone who wants to show you his strength, he grips your hand, for example, and squeezes it so that you cry out and show pain? Is it not courteous that you comply with him, saying "Ah!" and showing him, out of politeness, that he is stronger than you?

As for the meaning of ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ (21:83): whenever you see a group sharing an attribute, Allah includes Himself together with His creatures in it, as in ﴿the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ (21:83), and ﴿the best of creators﴾ (23:14), and ﴿the best of planners﴾ (3:54). So know that Allah, the Exalted, affirms the same attribute for His servants and does not diminish their share.

Mercy is therefore among the attributes of human beings, as the noble ḥadīth says: "Those who show mercy will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful."¹

And in: "Show mercy to those on earth, and He who is in heaven will show mercy to you."²

So mercy is a trait to be adopted from the characteristics of the Truth, glorified is He, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take on the characteristics of Allah."

Thus: creatures have the attribute of mercy, but Allah is the Most Merciful of all the merciful, because His mercy encompasses everything. As we said regarding the attribute of creation: you may, for instance, fashion a cup from sand and bring it into existence, and benefit from it; but can your creating of the cup be like the creating of Allah?

¹ Narrated by Aḥmad in his Musnad (2/160), al-Tirmidhī in his Sunan (1924), and Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan (4941), from the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. al-Tirmidhī said: "This ḥadīth is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."

² Narrated by Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilya (4/210), and al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr (10277) and al-Muʿjam al-Ṣaghīr (1/101), from the ḥadīth of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, with the wording: "Show mercy to whoever is on earth, and He who is in heaven will show mercy to you."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿So We responded to him and removed the affliction that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾

God responded to Job (Ayyub) in what he asked of Him, namely the removal of the harm that had befallen him, and He gave him more than that, an additional bounty (nafilah) he had not asked for, since he had been in a state of few family members and had no one to support him.

﴿a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ (al-Anbiya'): that every worshipper who sincerely devotes his worship to God, Exalted is He, may know that if harm or distress touches him and he turns to God, God will respond to him in what he desires and will give him, beyond the response, another bounty. What happened to the Prophet of God Job appears to be a model that ought to be emulated.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4507): (Scholars differed about the length of his period in affliction. Ibn 'Abbas said the period of affliction was seven years, seven months, seven days and seven nights. Wahb said thirty years, and al-Hasan said seven years and one month. I say: more correct than these, and God knows best, is eighteen years, related by Ibn Shihab from the Prophet (ﷺ), mentioned by Ibn al-Mubarak.)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 85:

We have said that Surat al-Anbiya' does not recount complete stories of the prophets; rather, it gives us a portion of them. Here it mentions Isma'il, Idris and Dhu al-Kifl by name only.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿Each of them was of the patient ones﴾ (al-Anbiya', 85). It is as if patience in itself is a reason for which Allah sends a messenger. Let us consider the patience of Isma'il, and how he was patient when his father was to slaughter him on account of a dream he had seen. What patience is greater than this?

Then he grew up in a valley without vegetation, and bore the hardships of this dry, barren environment, and submitted to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer...﴾ (Ibrahim, 37).

It is as if his leaving this land and seeking another land with luxury, crops and fruits would be a refusal to establish prayer. Therefore we see him preferring to remain in this place, and renouncing the luxuries of this world which others enjoy, in compliance with the command of Allah.

The result was that Allah gave him what is better than crops and fruits: a gift in which he takes pride among all the prophets, namely that He made from his offspring the final Prophet, Muhammad ibn Abdullah (ﷺ). And what fruit is better than this?

As for Idris: he was of the fifth generation of the descendants of Adam (peace be upon him). Some scholars say he is (Ouzouris), but we say only what the Qur'an says, (Idris). The people of the histories say: the Prophet of Allah Idris was the first whom Allah taught the spinning of wool and the sewing of garments; before that they used to cover their nakedness with pieces of hide.

He was also the first to use the stars to know directions and conditions, and the first to write with the pen. These are called "the firsts of Idris."

As for Dhu al-Kifl: al-Kifl means share and portion. So why was he named (Dhu al-Kifl)? Dhu al-Kifl was the son of Ayyub (peace be upon him). It appears that the sons of Ayyub were many; Allah singled out Dhu al-Kifl for prophethood, and this was his share to the exclusion of the other sons of Ayyub. Therefore he was named (Dhu al-Kifl)(1).

The root (kafl) also occurs in the saying of the True, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you two portions of His mercy...﴾ (al-Hadid, 28).

This verse came after the discussion of Isa (peace be upon him) and those who believed in him and followed him. The Exalted says: O you who have believed in the earlier messengers, the last of whom was Isa (peace be upon him), believe in the final Messenger so that you may have two portions, that is, two shares and two portions of Allah's mercy: the share of your faith in Isa and those before him of the messengers, and a share for your faith in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Then the Exalted describes them: ﴿Each of them was of the patient ones﴾ (al-Anbiya', 85). So He described all the prophets with patience, because they were exposed to various kinds of persecution, harm and terrors in the cause of their call, and they endured all of this.

1. Mujahid said regarding Dhu al-Kifl: he was a righteous man, not a prophet, who undertook for the prophet of his people that he would suffice him in the affairs of his people, establish them for him, and judge among them with justice, and he did so; hence he was named Dhu al-Kifl. (Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir, 3/190). Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4508) gave other opinions, among them:
He was a chaste man who took responsibility for everyone who fell into trouble, accusation or claim, and Allah would deliver him through his hands.
He was named Dhu al-Kifl because Allah guaranteed him, in his striving and work, double the reward of the other prophets of his time.
The mercy here means prophethood (nubuwwah). It is a great matter and a great bestowal. If they bear some hardships in its cause, there is no shame in that.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 87:

(Dhu al-Nun): He is our master Yunus ibn Matta, the companion of the fish. "Al-Nun" is one of the names of the fish, and its plural is "ninan," like "hut" (fish) and "hitan" (fishes); for this reason he was named by it. Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to the people of Nineveh (Ninawa) in the land of Mosul in Iraq.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Addas: "You are from the town of the righteous Prophet, Yunus ibn Matta."(1)

"Al-Nun" is also the name of a letter of the alphabet, but the name of the letter coincides with the name of something else, as in (Qaf), which is also the name of a mountain; likewise "al-Sin," for there is a river called al-Sin. Thus the names of the letters coincide with the names of things.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when he went off in anger...(87)﴾ (al-Anbiya), the root (gh-d-b) gives us the adjective for the singular: we say "ghadib" and "ghadban" (angry). But "mughadib" (one who is angry together with another) gives a different meaning, because it indicates mufa'ala (reciprocity), so there must be another person before you: you are angry and he is angry, like "sharaka fulan fulanan" (so-and-so shared with so-and-so).

However, in the principles of the language we give preference to the agent aspect in one of them and the patient aspect in the other, as when we say "shaarak Zayd 'Amran" (Zayd shared with 'Amr): the sharing occurred from both of them together, but the agent aspect is more pronounced on Zayd's side, so each of them is an agent at one time and an object at another.

Sometimes the language takes note of this reciprocity and bears both meanings together, the agent and the object, as in the saying of the Arab poet who describes travel through a land of scorpions, where if you pass through it without being harmed by the scorpions, they make peace with you and do not harm you. He says:

"The serpents have made peace with his foot,
the Afʿawan (2) and the large shuja' al-qashʿam (3)."

That is: he made peace with the serpents, and the serpents made peace with him, so the peace was from both of them together; but the side of the serpents prevailed, so they came as the agent, because their harm is stronger than his harm. Then, when he put "al-Afʿawan wa-l-shujaʿ al-qashʿam" in apposition to "al-hayyat" (the serpents), which are names of serpents, he should have put the apposition in the nominative, following the word it is in apposition to; yet he put it in the accusative, saying "al-Afʿawan wa-l-shujaʿ al-qashʿam," because he took into account that on the serpents' side they are also objects.

So for what was Dhu al-Nun angry? He was angry because his people denied him, so he threatened them that if they did not repent, punishment would descend upon them. The appointed time came and the punishment did not descend upon them as he had threatened, so he feared that they would deny him and become bold against him, and he left among them in anger, going to another place, while he did not know that they had repented, so God postponed their punishment and deferred their chastisement.

In another verse the Truth, glorified is He, clarifies this situation: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time.(98)﴾ (Yunus).

That is: before that, no town had come to faith and had its faith benefit it, except one town, the people of Yunus; they believed and repented, so God deferred their punishment.

Therefore: Yunus went out "mughadiban" (one who is angry together with others), not merely "ghadiban," because his people shared in it and were the cause of his anger, just as happened in the matter of the Prophet's emigration (hijra), peace be upon him. The Messenger of God emigrated from Mecca, but he did not abandon it (in the sense of hajr, rejecting it); it was called a hijra because the people of Mecca first rejected (hajaru) the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and rejected his call, and also compelled him to emigrate and leave Mecca. So they were a party to the emigration and its cause.

Therefore the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, addressing Mecca: ("By God, you are the best land of God and the land most beloved of God to me, and had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left.")(4)

Al-Mutanabbi(5) took up this meaning and expressed it in his saying:

"When you depart from a people who have decided
that you should not leave them, it is they who are the departing ones."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so he thought that We would not decree (upon) him...(87)﴾ (al-Anbiya): some look at the verse superficially and say: how could Yunus think that God would not be able to decree against him? This understanding arises from ignorance of the usages of the language. The meaning here is not capability over a thing and control of it. If you survey this root (q-d-r) in the Qur'an, you will find another meaning for it, as in His saying: ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth, and whoever has his provision restricted (qudira 'alayhi rizquhu), let him spend from what God has given him...(7)﴾ (al-Talaq). The meaning of "qudira 'alayhi rizquhu" is: his provision was constricted.

Among them is His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts (yaqdir)...(30)﴾ (al-Isra).

And His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and blesses him, he says, "My Lord has honored me." (15) But when He tests him and restricts his provision (qadara 'alayhi rizqahu), he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."(16)﴾ (al-Fajr).

So: His saying ﴿so he thought that We would not decree (upon) him...(87)﴾ means: when Yunus went out from his land in anger at his people, he thought that God would not constrict him, but would rather widen things for him and replace for him a better place than his land, as is evident from what He said after it: ﴿so he called out in the darknesses(6) that there is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers.(87)﴾ (al-Anbiya). He, glorified is He, wants to relieve his distress, and relief of distress is only by the attribute of power.

How, then, would the meaning be sound if we said: "He will not be able to decree against him," meaning: God is not able against Yunus?(7)

Therefore the meaning is: He will not constrict upon him, because he knew that he was a messenger from God, and that his Lord would not abandon him, nor forsake him, nor leave him in this distress.

A difficulty has been found regarding the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify (God), (143) he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.(144)﴾ (al-Saffat).

How could he remain in the belly of the fish until the Day of Resurrection, when Yunus would die, and the fish's term would come and it would die too? Or will the fish continue until the Day of Resurrection carrying Yunus in its belly?

Those people overlooked the theory of containment in mixtures. For instance, if you dissolve a cube of sugar in a glass of water, the molecules of water will contain the molecules of sugar; the greater contains the lesser. The sugar cube does not contain the water; rather the water contains the sugar.

So if the fish dies, and Yunus, peace be upon him, dies in its belly, and their atoms react and interpenetrate, then the fish has contained Yunus until the Hour arises, and on this the meaning remains correct, for he is in its belly despite the scattering of their atoms.(8)

The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said, "That is my brother; he was a prophet and I am a prophet." Then 'Addas bent over the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, kissing his head, his hands and his feet..
2 Al-Afʿawan: the male of the vipers (afa'i). Al-Qashʿam: the large one. (Lisan al-'Arab, roots f-ʿ-w and q-sh-ʿ-m).
3 Ibn Manzur cited it in Lisan al-'Arab (root sh-j-ʿ) attributing it to al-Ahmar, but with the wording "al-shuja' al-shujʿam," and said: al-Shujʿam: the large one among them; it was also said: the wicked, rebellious one among them. He then said: "The accusative of al-shuja' and al-afʿawan is by way of meaning the speech; for when the serpents make peace with the foot, the foot has made peace with them, so it is as if he said: the foot made peace with the serpents, then he made al-afʿawan an apposition to them."..
4 Recorded by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (3108), and al-Darimi in his Sunan (2/239), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Adi ibn Hamra' al-Zuhri who said: "I saw the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, standing on his mount at al-Hazwara, saying..................... the hadith.."
5 He is Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Kindi, Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, the wise poet and one of the glories of Arabic literature. Born in 303 AH in Kufa in the quarter of Kinda, he grew up in Syria, then traveled in the desert seeking literature, the Arabic sciences and the days of the Arabs. He came to Sayf al-Dawla al-Hamdani, ruler of Aleppo, and praised him, then went to Egypt, praised Kafur al-Ikhshidi, then satirized him. He was killed at al-Nu'maniyya, together with his son and his servant, in the year 354 AH (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/115)..
6 Ibn Mas'ud said: the darkness of the belly of the fish, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the night. Similarly it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Qatada. (Said by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 3/192)..
7 Al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir (6/4511): "This is a rejected, disavowed view, because it is disbelief. Al-Tha'labi mentioned, and 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr and many scholars said, its meaning is: he thought that We would not constrict upon him."..
8 Qatada said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to remain in its belly until the Day they are resurrected (144)﴾ (al-Saffat): the belly of the fish would become a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/127), attributing it to 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim)..

Allah answered the call of Yunus, peace be upon him, and saved him from distress. ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:88). So this is not specific to Yunus; it applies to every believer who calls upon Allah with this supplication. ﴿And thus...﴾ (21:88) means: such deliverance do We bring about for the believers who turn to Allah with this statement: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:87). Then Allah removes their grief and relieves their distress.

Therefore Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Thawwiru (stir up) the Qur'an," meaning: stir it up and search through its verses so that you extract its treasures and secrets (1).

Sayyidina Ja'far al-Sadiq was among those who stirred up the Qur'an and reflected upon it deeply, and he would draw from its verses a cure for every disease, serving, as we say, as a "prescription" (rawshita) for every condition of the believer.

The believer moves between many states, among them fear, whether the fear of losing the pleasures of this world or the fear of a tyrant who threatens him. He may also feel constriction and tightness in the chest without knowing its cause, and this is ghamm (grief). He may be exposed to the schemes of schemers, the plots of plotters, and the designs of the people of evil.

All of these are states that befall a person, in which he needs someone who supports him and brings him out of what he suffers, for he has no power or strength of his own, and cannot take precautions against all these matters.

The splendor and ornaments of this world may also tempt him, so he looks above what he is in and seeks more, and there is no end to human ambitions in this matter, as the poet said:
"His needs die with a man, while one need remains for him as long as he remains."

People are always eager to enjoy all the blessings and comforts of life, and in this they are mistaken, because the completion of a thing is the beginning of its decline, as the poet said:
"When something is complete, its deficiency appears; so await its decline once it is said to be complete."

For man is a child of changes, and no state endures for him, whether in health or sickness, wealth or poverty, sorrow or joy. Change is the mark of mankind, and glory be to Him who does not change. So what remains after you reach the peak, when you are a child of changes?

We see people become angry and complain if some of the comforts and pleasures of this world escape them, or life diminishes something for them, and they do not realize that this deficiency is what preserves the blessing for you and repels the evil eyes of the envious, so that what you have remains intact for you.

For example, you find a good family that has won the attention and respect of people, yet among them is a wicked, bad person who disparages the family. This person is the one who repels the eyes and envy of people from it.

Al-Mutanabbi took this meaning and expressed it in his praise of Sayf al-Dawla (2), saying:
"The people gaze upon your perfection, so seek refuge from the evil of their eyes in a single flaw."

Let us return to the "prescription" of Sayyidina Ja'far al-Sadiq, which he extracted for us from the Book of Allah, just as physicians extract medicines and remedies from the books of the wise:

He said: "I am amazed at one who fears and does not turn to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:173). For I have heard that Allah follows it immediately with: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and bounty; no harm touched them...﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:174)."

"And I am amazed at one who is grieved and does not turn to His saying: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:87). For I have heard that Allah follows it immediately with: ﴿So We responded to him and saved him from the distress, and thus do We save the believers﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:88)."

"And I am amazed at one who is plotted against and does not turn to His saying: ﴿And I entrust my affair to Allah...﴾ (Ghafir 40:44)."

"And I am amazed at one who seeks the world and its adornment and does not turn to His saying: ﴿What Allah willed; there is no power except by Allah...﴾ (al-Kahf 18:39). For I have heard that Allah follows it immediately with: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden...﴾ (al-Kahf 18:40)."

Thus it is incumbent upon the believer to be tranquil and confident in the companionship of Allah, and to be at ease, as we say, "with a summer watermelon in his belly," because he turns to his Lord with the appropriate supplication in every one of these states. When your Lord sees you turning to Him and humbly beseeching Him, and you attribute every blessing in yourself, your family, or your wealth to Allah and acknowledge the Bestower, glory be to Him, He will give you something better than it.

(1) In the hadith of Abdullah: "Stir up the Qur'an, for in it is the news of the former and the latter peoples." Shamir said: "Tathwir al-Qur'an is reciting it and discussing its exegesis and meanings with scholars." (Lisan al-Arab, root: th-w-r).
(2) He is: Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Hamdan, Abu al-Hasan Sayf al-Dawla al-Hamdani, the patron and patron-praised of al-Mutanabbi, born in Miyafariqin (in Diyar Bakr) in the year 303 AH, raised brave and refined with high aspiration. He held Wasit, Damascus and Aleppo, and died there in the year 356 AH at the age of 53. Al-A'lam by al-Zirikli (4/303).
(3) Inqalaba: returned and changed back to its original state, or to another state. Fa-inqalabu: i.e., they returned. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/129).

Then Allah, glorified is He, tells us about another of His prophets, saying: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾

Zakariyya, peace be upon him, had reached an advanced age, and Allah had not granted him a child, so he turned to Allah: ﴿He said, "My Lord, my bones have indeed weakened, and my head has flared with white hair, and I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord. And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing."﴾ (Maryam)

When Allah gave him the good news of a child, he marveled, because he looked at the means that bring things about and asked how Allah could grant him a child when he had reached such an advanced age and his wife was barren. So he wished to confirm this good news: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?" He said, "Thus it is; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I had already created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾ (Maryam)

Allah, exalted is He, reassures His prophet Zakariyya: set aside the worldly causes for creation, because the One who gives you good news is the Creator.

Zakariyya had learned from his guardianship of Maryam that Allah gives through means, and gives even when means are scarce. The people of Maryam had competed for her guardianship and raced to undertake this service, because they knew her nobility and station. So they cast lots for who would take charge of her: they brought their pens and cast them into the river (2), and the pen of Zakariyya emerged, and he won the guardianship of Maryam:

﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they cast their pens, (to see) which of them would be Maryam's guardian, nor were you with them when they disputed.﴾ (Al 'Imran)

The drawing of lots was for the importance of this matter and its great significance; and lots are a means of leaving matters to destiny, so that personal desires do not interfere in them.

When Zakariyya became Maryam's guardian, he would provide for her needs and look after her affairs. One day he entered upon her and found with her food that he had not brought, (3) ﴿He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ (Al 'Imran)

Here is a lesson and an indication of the necessity for the head of a household to follow up on his family: if he sees in the house something he did not bring, he should ask about its source. For the hand of the children may reach out to what is not theirs. This is the basis of the principle ("From where is this for you?") that we need to apply when we have doubts.

Zakariyya seized upon Maryam's answer, which came quickly and confidently, indicating the clear truth that does not waver: ﴿She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ (Al 'Imran)

Yes, this is a matter Zakariyya knew, but it had not been at the forefront of his awareness, and Maryam reminded him of it: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication."﴾ (Al 'Imran)

That is: since the matter is so, grant me a son who will inherit prophethood after me.

Then he mentions the grounds of his weakness and his old age, and that his wife is barren; these are grounds for prevention, not grounds for having children, because Allah provides for whom He wills without account and without means.

Thus Zakariyya benefited from this word, and Maryam also benefited from it afterward, when pregnancy came to her with the Messiah without the worldly causes.

Here Zakariyya calls upon his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors.﴾ (al-Anbiya): That is: I do not ask for a child to inherit my kingdom after me; You are the best of inheritors, who inherits the earth and the heavens, and to You belongs everything.

1 Al-mawali here means: relatives, paternal cousins and the agnatic kin who are nearest to him in lineage. Said by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4248).
2 Narrated by 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, Qatada, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others, that they went to the River Jordan and cast lots there, each throwing his pen, and whichever pen stood firm in the current would be her guardian. They threw their pens, and the water carried them off except the pen of Zakariyya, which remained. It is said that it went upstream, cutting against the flow of the water. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1/363).
3 That is: he found with her summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. Said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Awfi. Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (1/360).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 21, verse 90:

The answer of Allah to Zakariyya was not only that He granted him a child in his old age when his wife was barren. He also named him, and Allah the Exalted has a secret in this naming. This is because people are free in assigning names to the things named, as we have said, so there is no objection to naming a Black girl "Qamar" (moon), since the name leaves its original meaning and becomes a proper noun (ʿalam) for this named person. Thus there is a difference between the name and the one named.

Names are sometimes given as an omen (tafāʾul) that the named will be such, as when someone named his son Yahya (John), and it appears that he was suffering from the death of his children. Therefore he said:

"I named him Yahya, hoping he would live,
but there is no way to repel the decree of Allah concerning him."

That is: I named him Yahya in hope that he would live, but Allah's decree did not turn away from him.

Likewise, when ʿAbd al-Muttalib named Muhammad (ﷺ) he said: "I named him Muhammad so that he would be praised in the earth and in the heavens."(1)

But when one is named Yahya by the One who possesses life and possesses death, the name must be a name that matches its bearer, and he must live, so that even if he dies he dies as a martyr, so that life is realized for him even after death.

The meaning of ﴿We granted him...﴾ (21:90) is: We gave him without the law of human generation and without causes.

Then He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And We made his wife fit for him...﴾ (21:90). After she had been barren and unable to bear, We performed a divine operation that restored to her the matter of childbearing, because a woman bears as long as there are ova in her which form the embryo. When these ova are finished, she becomes sterile. These ova are in a cluster, with a specific number, like the cluster of eggs in a hen. For this reason they call the last of the children "the last of the cluster" (ākhir al-ʿunqūd).

Thus Yahya came into being without the cosmic causes of birth, because the Creator, glorified be He, willed it.

But why did He not say "We made you fit" to Zakariyya? They said: because a righteous man remains capable of fathering as long as he is able to perform the sexual act, however old he becomes, unlike the woman who receives, in whom the cessation occurs.

We see in those afflicted with sterility and non-begetting signs of the signs of Allah: a couple are both sound, their organs fit for reproduction, yet they do not conceive; then if each of them marries another spouse, they conceive, because the matter is not a mechanism, but behind the apparent causes is the will and purpose of Allah.

Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He grants to whom He wills females, and He grants to whom He wills males. Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren...﴾ (42:49-50).

Then the verses clarify the reason and cause of Allah's honouring and answering His prophet Zakariyya (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they would call upon Us in hope and fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us.﴾ (21:90)

These are three attributes that qualified Zakariyya and his wife for this divine gift. We must stand before this experience of our master Zakariyya, for it is not specific to him, but applies to every believer who offers these attributes from himself.

Therefore I say to whoever suffers from sterility and non-begetting, whom the means of this world have straitened, and who has knocked on the doors of doctors: let him turn to Allah with what Zakariyya and his family turned with (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they would call upon Us in hope and fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us.﴾ (21:90). Take this as a divine prescription (rūshita), and the answer will not fail you, by Allah's permission.

But why this particular attribute: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds...﴾ (21:90)?

They said: because you notice that those afflicted with sterility and non-begetting are often stingy and tight-fisted, having nothing that encourages them to spend, so they consider it too much to give anything to a poor person, because he is not their child.

When such a person hastens to spend and hastens to good deeds in all their kinds, he has challenged nature and gone against it in this matter. Perhaps those whom Allah has tested with sterility incline to resentment towards others, or harbour rancour against those who bear children. But when they cast off this resentment and look upon the children of others as their own, showing them compassion and hastening to good deeds, and then turn to Allah in supplication with hope and fear, then Allah the Exalted, who is the Supreme Creator, breaks for them the laws and regulations and grants them a child from where they do not reckon.

The meaning of ﴿and they were humbly submissive to Us﴾ (21:90) is: they were content with Our decree concerning them, content with sterility as a trial and a decree. A decree is not lifted from the servant until he is content with it. The believer should not rebel against the decree of Allah, and humility (khushūʿ) includes submitting to the decrees of creation among people.

1 On the authority of Abu al-Hakam al-Tanukhi, who said: "When the seventh day came (after the birth of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ), ʿAbd al-Muttalib slaughtered for him and invited the Quraysh. When they had eaten, they said: 'O ʿAbd al-Muttalib, what did you name this son of yours whom you have honoured us by presenting?' He said: 'I named him Muhammad.' They said: 'Why did you turn away from the names of his family?' He said: 'I wanted Allah to praise him in the heavens and His creation to praise him on the earth.'" Related by al-Bayhaqi in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwa* (1/113), and Ibn ʿAsakir in *Tahdhib Tarikh Dimashq al-Kabir* (1/282), and transmitted by Ibn Kathir in *al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya* (2/264).

Would you like to know why Lady Maryam (Mary) is mentioned among the procession of prophets? We say: because prophethood is God's choosing of a prophet from among God's creation, and His choosing Maryam over all the women of the worlds, so that she would bear a child without a male, is a kind of choosing. This is a choosing specific to Maryam alone among the women of the worlds, because the choosing of prophets has been repeated, whereas the choosing of Maryam for this matter has never been repeated for anyone else.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:91]: it means she preserved and guarded her chastity, so she did not let anyone have access to her.(1)

As for the meaning of ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:91]: it means a matter specific to her, outside the law of nature. There is in the matter no male or pairing; rather, the breath which God breathed into Adam, from which all these souls came, is the very breath He breathed into Maryam, from which came one soul. The spirit is the very one of which God said: ﴿And when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit...﴾ [al-Hijr 15:29].

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:91]: it means a wondrous thing in the universe. The wonder in her is that she bore a child without a male, and the wonder in him is that he was born without a father. Both of them are a sign from God and a miracle.

(1) Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4518): "It is said that the intended meaning of 'farj' is the opening of the shirt, i.e., no suspicion clung to her garment, meaning she was pure in her garments. The openings of a shirt are four: the two sleeve-openings, the upper and the lower. Al-Suhayli said: Do not let your mind go to anything other than this, for it is of subtle metaphor, since the Qur'an is more exalted in meaning, more balanced in wording, more refined in allusion, and more beautiful in expression than to intend what the mind may go to."

(2) That is: in the collar of her garment. This was said by Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari in Fath al-Rahman (p. 271). Qatada said: he breathed into her collar. Muqatil said: he breathed into her private part. Both are mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/671). The dir' is a woman's garment.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 21, verse 92:

Then, after recounting scenes from the procession of the prophets, the Truth (may He be glorified) says:

﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ (92)

Ummah (أمة): a group bound together by a single tie, whether of land, of a king's rule, or of religion, as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿We found our fathers following a community...﴾ (22) [al-Zukhruf], meaning: following a religion.

The meaning, then, is: this community of yours is one community, in that it is one, with no disagreement among it, and the messengers all came to complete one edifice, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of me and the prophets before me is that of a man who built a house and made it beautiful and perfect, except for the place of one brick in a corner. So people went around it, marvelling at it, and saying: 'Why was this brick not put in place?' He said: 'I am the brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets.'"(2)

The meaning is that through him (ﷺ) prophethood is completed and sealed.

The term ummah is also applied to a man who combines all the virtues of goodness, because God (exalted is He) has scattered the qualities of goodness among creation, so that there is no one who gathers all talents and excellences. Rather, each of us has a distinction and a virtue in some aspect, so that people complete one another and need one another, and interconnection arises among the elements of society. This interconnection happens either through voluntary needs or through compelled needs.

So if all people were to learn and graduate from the university, then who would do the trades and other crafts? Who will sweep the streets and handle such matters? If the sewage channels were blocked, would these doctors and professors gather to repair them? And even if they repaired them once, that would be voluntary.

As for public interests, they are not sustained by volunteering; they are sustained by need and compulsion. Were it not for this need, the sanitation worker would not go out in the morning to this hard, repellent work; but how could he not, with the responsibility of a family, children and expenses on his neck?

We have already said: a person should not be deceived by the talents and distinctions he has, nor should he exalt himself with them over the creation of God. He should ask about what others have of talents that he needs and cannot perform himself.

So: need is the bond in society. If it were only volunteering and favour, we would achieve nothing. If we said to the worker, "Be kind enough to sweep the street," he would find a thousand excuses to offer. But if his children would die of hunger should he not work, there is no doubt he would hasten and take the initiative.

The truth is that each individual in society serves only himself: just as you benefit others, you benefit from them. Therefore, beware of envying the one who excels in some matter, for his excellence ultimately returns to your benefit.

Just as we say these matters concerning worldly affairs, we say them concerning the affairs of the Hereafter. When we see the person of religiosity, and the person of good character and commitment, we do not mock him or ridicule him as some like to do, for his righteousness will return to your benefit, and you will profit from his piety and uprightness, and perhaps we are provided for because of such people.

It may be that in a single household there are thugs, clever people and educated people, and among them is a disabled person, a madman, or one who is absorbed (majdhub). You see everyone despising him and belittling his standing, or you see him cast out and shunned among them, no one honored by knowing him, while perhaps they all live in his shade and are provided for through his blessing.

We often see people angry and resentful at the decree of God when He grants them a child with a defect or disability. By God, if you were content with it and accepted God's decree concerning him, he would be for you a complete shade.

These people were created this way for a wisdom: so that we do not rebel against God's handiwork in His creation, and so that those of comfort, safety and health feel God's favour upon them. Let us know that God (exalted is He) does not take anything from His servant except that He has given him a substitute for it.

You may also observe, for example, the condition of the majdhub people whom you see in every place, neglected, whom people look down on and recoil from their tattered appearance. Yet you see the people of rank and authority, when hardship befalls them and means fail them, resort to such majdhub folk, seeking from them blessing and prayer. This in itself is the highest thing that people of rank and authority and influence can aspire to: that their word be heard and their command obeyed, and that people turn to them as they turned to this poor majdhub.

When God causes good to come through the hand of this majdhub shaykh, you see the great lord seeking his blessing, inviting him to his food, warding off people's harm from him and embracing him, because he has tested him and knows that he has an outpouring from God's outpouring and a dignity which God singles out for whomever He wills of His servants. We are all servants of God; there is none among us who is a son of God, nor does anyone have kinship with God.

If reason is the dearest thing a human takes pride in, and is his adornment and ornament, you may look at the madman who has lost reason and been deprived of this precious faculty, and you see people pointing at him: "This is a madman." Yes, he is mad, but look at his conduct: have you seen a madman steal? Have you seen a madman commit adultery? Have you seen a madman take his own life?

So: despite being mad, he is fully aware of himself, because his Creator (mighty and majestic is He), though He took away his reason, gave him an instinct that governs him, just as instinct governs animals. Have you ever seen a donkey throw itself in front of a train, for example?

So: we must not belittle these people, nor look down on them, for God has compensated them for what He took from them. Among us are those who strive to reach what they have reached and cannot. And which of us does not wish to be like this majdhub whom people seek blessing from and ask for prayer? What greatness could a person seek beyond this? It is enough that he is not asked about what he does in this world, nor is he asked about it in the Hereafter.

Let us return to the words of God: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community...﴾ (92) [al-Anbiya']. Among the meanings of ummah: the man who combines all the qualities of goodness. Therefore God described His prophet Abraham as an ummah, saying: ﴿Indeed Abraham was an ummah...﴾ (120) [al-Nahl].

That is: he combined of the qualities of goodness what is found only in a complete community.

A community is not one unless its organizing system proceeds from one God. If its formation were from many, each god would go off with what it created, and they would overpower one another, and affairs would be corrupted. So as He (exalted is He) said: ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted...﴾ (71) [al-Mu'minun].

A community is not one unless it receives its commands from one God and submits to one object of worship. If it forgets this one God, it becomes discordant and scattered.

It is as if the Truth (exalted is He) says: You will be one community, through which you will rule the world, and your call will set out from an unlettered community that knows no culture and no learning, and has not been trained in governing nations, because it was a tribal community, each tribe with its own law, sovereignty and leadership.

Then there descends to you a system that gathers the whole world with its civilizations: a system that folds under its wing the civilization of Persia and the civilization of Rome and subdues them. Had you been a cultured community, they would have said, "a civilizational leap." But this is an unlettered community, and its prophet too is unlettered.
